10-65.summary: A fortnight of search-and-destroy patrolling by 1 RAR in September 1965, finding and destroying Viet Cong camps and clashing with small local-force groups.
10-65.text:
In September 1965 the Australian government lifted the restriction that had kept the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), to defending Bien Hoa Air Base, and the battalion could now be used in search-and-destroy operations, patrolling and security operations alongside the US 173rd Airborne Brigade[1]. Operation 10/65 followed in the same month, running from 14 to 27 September.

The record holds 64 contacts in the operation, all of them 1 RAR's. Most were finds of enemy camps and installations (25) and clashes on patrol (22), with a few sightings, bursts of harassing fire and two mines or booby traps. The Viet Cong met were mostly local-force men in small groups, who usually got away: on 15 September a section of 8 Platoon, C Company, came upon three in a clearing, killed one and drove the others off when they came back for his body. A grenade hidden in a hut roof wounded an Australian and two New Zealand members of an artillery forward observer party as A Company destroyed a camp, and on 21 September a sniper killed a soldier of A Company's 3 Platoon.

In all one Australian was recorded killed and five wounded, two of them New Zealanders, and 4 enemy killed and 8 wounded.

12-65.summary: 1 RAR's operation into the Iron Triangle in October 1965, where mines and booby traps caused most of its casualties.
12-65.text:
Operation 12/65, from 8 to 13 October 1965, is called Operation Iron Triangle in the record's accounts of its contacts. The Iron Triangle was a Viet Cong stronghold, and within it, about 40 kilometres from Saigon, lay the Cu Chi tunnel system[1].

The record holds 33 contacts, all of them involving the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR). Ten were mines or booby traps, more than any other kind, and eight were harassing fire. On the first day men of C Company's 8 Platoon, riding in armoured personnel carriers, struck an anti-tank mine made from a 105mm shell, which injured nine Australians and killed the American driver; later booby traps wounded men of A, B and C Companies, and the platoon commanders' lessons were about spacing men more widely. A sniper killed a soldier reconnoitring a track on 9 October. The Australians also struck back: C Company's 7 Platoon killed three Viet Cong creeping up on its harbour, and B Company's 5 Platoon assaulted a defended village that proved to be an administrative headquarters with 23 tunnels, weapon pits and booby-trapped approaches, and called in an air strike on it.

The record counts 2 killed on the allied side, one of them the American driver, and 24 wounded, among them a New Zealand gunner and a Vietnamese policeman; 11 enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

new-life.summary: 1 RAR clears Viet Cong villages around Vo Dat, taking Chanh Duc and Vo Xu, detaining many suspects and seizing tons of rice.
new-life.text:
Operation New Life ran from 21 November to 14 December 1965 (the record also numbers it 16/65). Vo Xu, one of its villages, where the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), searched for and detained suspected Viet Cong, lay in Binh Tuy province[1].

After securing the road from Vo Dat to Chanh Duc, the battalion assaulted a hill called the Brass Monkey after air and artillery bombardment on 22 November, and found it deserted. On 24 November D Company attacked Chanh Duc village, fought off a group near the church and cleared along the road, and seven Viet Cong were recorded killed. Two days later C Company, mounted in the carriers of 1 APC Troop, made a frontal assault down the road into Vo Xu and took it quickly. The battalion cleared the northern part of Chanh Duc, Duc Hanh, detaining thirty-nine people, and went back into Vo Xu, where 52 Viet Cong were captured; a force of just under a platoon firing from across the La Nga river wounded two Australians of B Company's 4 Platoon, one of whom died. The companies detained 40 more suspects and found caches of rice, one of 20 tons, which was taken to Vo Dat for the local people.

December was quieter: more rice caches, a booby trap, a sighting and a Viet Cong who came over to C Company. The record holds 22 contacts, 20 of them 1 RAR's, with engineers in the others. One Australian was recorded killed and one wounded, and 15 enemy killed.

sources.title: Australian infantry serving during the Vietnam War

1-66.summary: 1 RAR's costliest operation of its first tour, in January 1966, as it came upon the Viet Cong's tunnels, snipers and booby traps.
1-66.text:
Operation 1/66 ran from 2 to 13 January 1966, and one of its contacts is recorded under the name Crimp. The Australian War Memorial describes Operation Crimp, from 8 to 14 January, as a search-and-destroy operation in the Hobo Woods north of Saigon, in which the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), uncovered the Cu Chi tunnel complex[1]. Some 8,000 troops of the US 1st Infantry Division and 173rd Airborne Brigade took part, with 1 RAR dropped as a blocking force on the northern edge; the allies found few Viet Cong above ground, while snipers caused a steadily rising number of casualties, until it became clear that the enemy was underground[2].

The record holds 32 contacts, all 1 RAR's, and shows that kind of fighting. On 8 January a command-detonated mine killed an officer of B Company's headquarters, and a sniper in the same clump of bamboo shot a radio operator and later killed a machine-gunner. On 10 January an engineer corporal died of gas and lack of air in a tunnel that engineers were filling with smoke and tear gas to find its other entrances, and documents and caches of food and medical stores were found; the same day 12 Platoon, D Company, walked into an ambush fired from bunkers, and two medics were killed going forward to the wounded. On 13 January D Company cleared a heavily fortified trench system and ran into booby traps. The Australians also ambushed and killed two Viet Cong coming to a group of huts.

The record counts 7 killed on the Task Force's side and 10 wounded, and 12 enemy killed. By the time Crimp ended on 14 January, the number of Australian dead in South Vietnam had doubled from 8 to 16[2].

sources.title: Clearing Vietcong tunnels during the Vietnam War

4-66.summary: 1 RAR guards US engineers building a road in February 1966, and its night ambushes and pickets catch Viet Cong groups moving around them.
4-66.text:
Operation 4/66, from 20 to 25 February 1966, is called Operation Rolling Stone in several of the record's accounts. Because of its successful patrolling, the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), was asked by the US 1st Infantry Division to take part in Rolling Stone, which the Australian War Memorial dates 19 to 26 February; the battalion provided security for US Army engineers building a road, and afterwards returned to the 173rd Airborne Brigade[1].

The record holds 23 contacts, 20 of them 1 RAR's. Most came at night, as small Viet Cong groups moved around the battalion's positions: on 23 February a C Company picket killed two of a group that stopped 20 metres from its machine-gun, and the next day 9 Platoon drove off Viet Cong digging an ambush position of eight pits on a track. On the night of 24 February an ambush by 1 Section, 4 Platoon, B Company, engaged, by its company commander's count, 28 Viet Cong without taking fire in return, killing four and capturing two wounded, while around C Company's positions a standing patrol and 9 Platoon killed intruders.

The record counts one Australian wounded, and 14 enemy killed and 3 wounded.

silver-city.summary: 1 RAR and attached American units are flown across the Song Be in March 1966, and fight Viet Cong groups around the rice caches they find.
silver-city.text:
Operation Silver City ran from 9 to 22 March 1966. It opened with the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's (1 RAR's) Assault Pioneer Platoon crossing the Song Be in fog to secure a landing zone for American infantry and artillery; one Australian was killed at the crossing by Viet Cong on the far bank, and by mid-morning the battalion and its attached US units had been flown in.

The record holds 50 contacts, 37 of them 1 RAR's and others the US armoured unit attached to the battalion. Much of the work was finding and clearing caches of rice, and the Viet Cong fought for them: on 15 March 2 Platoon, A Company, held off 20 to 25 enemy at a night ambush, and a patrol of C Company's 7 Platoon ran into an L-shaped ambush by more than 25 well-armed Viet Cong, losing one man killed; on 16 March 2 Platoon, guarding engineers clearing booby traps from a cache of about 420 bags of rice, fought about 25 Viet Cong of the mobile force for five minutes. A Claymore mine wounded two Australian engineers of 3 Field Troop and an American on a vehicle carrying rice out of a cache.

In all the record counts 2 killed, both Australians, and 12 wounded on the allied side, and 21 enemy killed and 10 wounded, six of each estimated from an air strike on a group the American armoured unit had met. One contact was friendly fire.

abilene.summary: 1 RAR sweeps around the Binh Ba airstrip and rubber plantation, and its night ambushes catch Viet Cong on the tracks.
abilene.text:
Operation Abilene ran from 30 March to 15 April 1966 (the record also numbers it 7/66), for the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), with its armoured personnel carrier troop. Its contacts were around the Binh Ba airstrip and its rubber plantation, and near Long Tan.

The record holds 34 contacts, 32 of them 1 RAR's, half of them on patrol. On 2 April the deputy commander of the US 1st Division, landing at Binh Ba, saw Viet Cong moving away; B Company and 1 APC Troop gave chase in their carriers and killed two, and the sweeps around the airstrip that day took 28 detainees. The battalion's night ambushes then caught Viet Cong on the tracks: 4 Platoon killed two at a track junction on 2 April, a ten-man ambush of 11 Platoon killed three on 4 April, and 8 Platoon's ambush on a moonlit track the next night left four blood trails. In several of these the Viet Cong did not fire back. An American armoured personnel carrier was destroyed by recoilless-rifle fire near Long Tan.

No one on the allied side was recorded killed and 5 were wounded, two Australians by a booby trap and two Americans in the carrier attack, and 13 enemy were recorded killed and 13 wounded.

denver.summary: 1 RAR is flown to Song Be in April 1966 to clear the Viet Cong from its rubber plantations and jungle.
denver.text:
For Operation Denver the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), was flown from its base at Bien Hoa to the airstrip at Song Be in Caribou aircraft, and pushed out through extensive rubber plantations and jungle to clear the Viet Cong from the area; the Australian War Memorial calls it the battalion's seventh major mission of the year[1]. The record has it from 14 to 22 April 1966.

The record holds 23 contacts, 22 of them 1 RAR's, mostly brief clashes with small groups. On 14 April, as B Company moved into a harbour, 5 Platoon caught three Viet Cong walking up the ridge towards it and killed two, and a clearing patrol of D Company met eight Viet Cong with automatic weapons, who wounded an Australian and got away. On 21 April a section of D Company's 12 Platoon met a group at close range and wounded three; the platoon commander noted that men hit by the new M16 rifle ran on as if unhurt. Patrols detained Viet Cong and suspects and found medical supplies and supply lists in huts.

The record counts one Australian wounded, and 3 enemy killed and 5 wounded.

sources.title: Vietnam. 1966-04-16. Australian troops move from the airstrip at Song Be, into Operation Denver

hardihood.summary: The Task Force's first operation: clearing and resettling the villages of Long Phuoc and Long Tan to secure the ground around the new base at Nui Dat.
hardihood.text:
Operation Hardihood was the Task Force's first task in Phuoc Tuy: making the ground safe for its new base at Nui Dat. The villages nearest the base, Long Tan and Long Phuoc, were considered Viet Cong strongholds, and everyone living within about 4 kilometres of a line around the base, Line Alpha, was to be moved out[1]. With the US 173rd Airborne Brigade and the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR), the newly arrived 5th Battalion (5 RAR) removed the villagers, their livestock and their possessions and resettled them at Hoa Long, Dat Do and Long Dien[1]. Moving them out made it much harder for the Viet Cong to gather information about the base and the Australians' movements, but because it was done without compensation it set back efforts to win the people's support[1].

The record dates Hardihood from 1 May to 24 June 1966 and holds 90 contacts, 73 of them 5 RAR's; the rest belong to the Task Force's headquarters and supporting units, to 6 RAR, arriving in June, and to 1 RAR. Most were patrols (42), security (18) and ambushes (10), and most were small: a platoon of D Company meeting eight enemy and killing three, a section surprised on a track by about six. One Australian was killed on 24 May, shot by his own side during what may have been a contact with the enemy. In June the enemy's mortars reached the Australians: on 10 June 120 mm and 82 mm mortar fire killed two men of a 5 RAR patrol and wounded four, and two days later D Company, sweeping north-east of Hoa Long for the mortar positions, had one man killed and three wounded; radar placed those mortars in Long Phuoc. In all the record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 11 wounded, and 16 enemy killed and 16 wounded.

The Viet Cong's tunnels and bunkers under Long Phuoc let them stay on after the villagers had gone, and when the mortar attacks continued, 6 RAR was sent to search, clear and destroy the empty village in Operation Enoggera, from 21 June[1].

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

smithfield.summary: The Battle of Long Tan: D Company, 6 RAR, holds off a far larger force in a rubber plantation near Nui Dat until relieved in armoured personnel carriers.
smithfield.text:
By August 1966 the base at Nui Dat was three months old, and the resettlement of Long Tan and Long Phuoc had given the enemy a reason to attack it[1]. In the days before, radio signals pointed to strong North Vietnamese forces within 5 kilometres of the base, though patrols found nothing, and on the night of 16 and 17 August the base was shelled by mortars and recoilless rifles[1]. Companies went out to find the firing points, and on 18 August D Company of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), took over the search and made for the Long Tan rubber plantation, a few kilometres from the base[1].

The record names this Operation Smithfield. D Company, 108 strong, was following fresh tracks east of Nui Dat when 11 Platoon met a few Viet Cong and then a much larger force. From about 5.30 pm the company was attacked in heavy rain under machine-gun and mortar fire; close artillery fire broke up many of the attacks, low cloud ruled out air strikes, and helicopters flew in ammunition. A Company rode out from Nui Dat in the armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, 1 APC Squadron, clashing on the way with the support company of the D445 Battalion and then with two companies of the 275th Regiment, and reached D Company after 7 pm as the enemy withdrew; B Company, heading back to the base, was turned round and joined them that evening. The record counts 17 killed on the Task Force's side and 23 wounded in the operation, and 265 enemy killed, 245 of them in D Company's fight. D Company's commander afterwards reported that the M60 machine-guns had jammed in the mud and that the men needed to carry more ammunition.

Captured documents and prisoners suggested that D Company had faced some 2,500 enemy, among them the Viet Cong 275th Main Force Regiment, at least one North Vietnamese battalion and the local D445 Battalion[1]. The Anzac Portal counts 18 Australians killed and 24 wounded, all but one of the dead from D Company[1]. Over the next days the companies searched the battlefield, finding traces of camps, supplies and graves; the enemy was not pursued, and the battalion returned to Nui Dat, ending the operation on 21 August[1].

queanbeyan.summary: 5 RAR searches the steep, cave-riddled Nui Thi Vai hills, where snipers and booby traps cost three Australian lives in a week.
queanbeyan.text:
Queanbeyan was one of two search-and-destroy operations the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), carried out in October 1966 in the Nui Thi Vai and Nui Toc Tien hills, north-west of the Nui Dinh hills; the other was Canberra[1]. It is steep ground, cut by watercourses, with granite outcrops, caves and cliff faces under dense forest, where movement on foot is difficult and slow[1].

The record holds 10 contacts from 17 to 24 October, all 5 RAR's, and they show how well the enemy used that ground. On the first day a booby trap wounded four men of A Company, and the Anti-Tank Platoon, guarding battalion headquarters, was pinned down by a skilful sniper and a machine-gun and had a man killed trying to clear a spur. On 18 October a lone sniper killed a sentry of the Assault Pioneer Platoon as it searched inhabited, booby-trapped caves; the next day two of its men were wounded by a buried mine near the caves, and the Anti-Tank Platoon, sent to free men pinned down by a sniper, was itself caught by snipers in the trees and machine-guns in the gullies, and a section leader was killed. The commanders were struck by the enemy's fire control: probably no more than ten men, firing from four or five directions and never twice from the same spot.

On 21 October 10 Platoon of D Company found two well-hidden huts, surrounded them and opened fire on a group of 18, killing ten. In all the record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 10 wounded, and 11 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 'Red Rats' and Phuoc Tuy
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

ingham.summary: 6 RAR and the armoured personnel carriers search along the Song Rai river for the Viet Cong's D445 Battalion, meeting ambushes, command-detonated mines and booby traps.
ingham.text:
Ingham was a battalion-scale search-and-destroy operation along the Song Rai river, between Nui Dat and Xuyen Moc, directed at the Viet Cong's D445 Provincial Mobile Battalion[1]. For it the 101st Field Battery was moved by Chinook helicopter for the first time[1].

The 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), with the armoured personnel carriers of 1 APC Squadron, made 37 contacts from 19 November to 2 December: 28 were 6 RAR's and 8 the carriers'. Most were patrols (29). On 21 November a patrol of C Company, fired on from ambush pits along a track, flanked them and found a camp with booby-trapped tunnels and a dead section commander of the D445 Battalion. On 25 November the enemy fired command-detonated mines at the carriers of 2 Troop; the carriers followed and killed two, but more mines that afternoon wounded three infantrymen inside. On 29 November five enemy fired on an Assault Pioneer Platoon in its night harbour when a sentry challenged them, killing one Australian and wounding two.

The operation's worst day was its last. On 2 December a command-detonated mine went off against D Company, killing one Australian and wounding ten, and three civilians were also wounded; about half the casualties, the man killed among them, came from an Australian Claymore mine carried by a non-commissioned officer, which went off in the blast. The record also notes evidence that a Vietnamese woman who ran to the scene was wounded or killed by soldiers who took her for an enemy. In all it counts 2 killed on the Task Force's side and 21 wounded, and 12 enemy killed and 16 wounded.

beaumaris.summary: A 5 RAR cordon and search in which a booby trap, probably laid by friendly forces, killed three men at a company orders meeting.
beaumaris.text: Beaumaris was a cordon and search by the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), on 14 February 1967; the record does not say which village. It holds a single contact, and a costly one: C Company's headquarters set off a booby trap while holding an orders meeting, and three Australians were killed and five wounded. The record says the mine was probably a booby trap laid by friendly forces.

bribie.summary: 6 RAR, flown in to cut off a Viet Cong force withdrawing from Phuoc Hai, runs into a dug-in D445 Battalion position and loses eight men killed.
bribie.text:
Operation Bribie was planned and organised in haste on 17 February 1967, as an attempt to destroy a communist force that had attacked the village of Lang Phuoc Hai, on the coast, earlier that day[1]. The 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), and the armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, were ordered to cut off the enemy's withdrawal, expecting to meet small, scattered groups heading back to their jungle bases[1]. The Australian War Memorial's history of the 101st Field Battery, which fired in support, says instead that the enemy had ambushed a South Vietnamese convoy[2].

6 RAR was flown in by helicopter near the abandoned settlement of Ap My An[1]. As 2 Platoon of A Company pushed into the jungle to secure the landing zone it ran into a dug-in company of D445 Battalion, with its heavy weapons company, in bunkers with overhead cover; six men were wounded and the platoon pulled back. B Company was ordered to assault the position with A Company's support, and after artillery fire it attacked and was pinned down by fire from all sides, from heavy machine-guns, Claymore mines and light mortars. Four air strikes were made, and 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came in to recover the casualties; one carrier was disabled by three recoilless rifle rounds, which killed its driver. After a four-hour battle the companies withdrew into a night position 200 metres away, and the enemy withdrew overnight. The commanding officer said he had not launched a full battalion attack because he had been ordered to finish at last light, and that the action showed the need for tanks.

The record counts 8 killed on the Task Force's side and 28 wounded, and 58 enemy killed. The Anzac Portal gives 27 wounded, and says official estimates put the enemy dead at between 50 and 70, though no one really knew; some of the Australian survivors felt the day had been a defeat[1]. The losses of Bribie and of Renmark, four days later, shocked the small Australian force and fed the thinking of senior officers who believed a third battalion and tanks were needed[3].

sources.title: Australian Armoured units serving during the Vietnam War

renmark.summary: A 5 RAR operation against the Long Hai hills, cancelled after a carrier hit a mine and men running to help set off more, killing nine Australians.
renmark.text:
Renmark was a search-and-destroy operation by the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), in the Long Hai hills, on the coast south of Nui Dat; the 103rd Field Battery supported it from a wood at the foot of the hills and from near the ruined village of Hoi My[1].

The record's first contacts, on 19 February 1967, were small: 4 Platoon of B Company met two Viet Cong near a platoon-sized camp and had a man wounded, and another was wounded by a booby trap as the camp was destroyed; the Reconnaissance Platoon met a group of four twice and killed a Viet Cong woman. On 21 February B Company was being carried by 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, into position for a Task Force attack on the Viet Cong stronghold of the Long Hai Hills when the leading carrier hit a powerful mine on a dirt track, killing two cavalrymen and two infantrymen. When no ambush followed, soldiers ran from their carriers to help the medics and set off more anti-personnel mines, killing or wounding most of the medics and the company headquarters; normal mine drills had been ignored. Engineers ordered everyone to keep still while they cleared the mines, the wounded were flown out by helicopter, and the operation was cancelled. The record counts 9 killed on the Task Force's side and 28 wounded, 26 of them in the minefield, and one enemy killed.

The Anzac Portal gives 7 killed and 26 wounded, all victims of mines and booby traps, with no enemy seen until the damage had been done[2]. With Bribie four days before, the losses shocked the small force and fed the thinking of senior officers who believed a third battalion and tanks were needed in South Vietnam[2].

sources.title: Australian Armoured units serving during the Vietnam War

leeton.summary: The barrier fence and minefield are built from the Horseshoe to the coast, with 5 RAR holding the Horseshoe, at a heavy cost to the engineers laying the mines.
leeton.text:
In March 1967 the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR) was given the task of setting up and defending a base on the rim of an extinct volcano known as the Horseshoe, to deny the Viet Cong access to supplies from the province[1]. The Task Force built its barrier minefield during Operation Leeton, from 3 March to 1 June 1967, running for about ten kilometres from the Horseshoe, north of Dat Do, to the coast north-east of Lang Phuoc Hai[2]. The Task Force's commander, Brigadier Stuart Graham, believed it would cut a vital Viet Cong supply route, stopping the enemy moving from their bases in the hills to the rice-growing areas and shielding the villagers from their influence; about 20,000 'jumping jack' mines, fitted with anti-lift devices, were to lie between two wire fences, guarded by Australian and South Vietnamese troops[3]. Its purpose was to safeguard the rice harvest and cut the enemy's main forces off from the people, because the patrolling needed without it was more than the Task Force could keep up[4].

The record's contacts under Leeton run from 6 March to 30 May, 11 of them. Most were 5 RAR's (7), whose soldiers helped put up the fence at the Horseshoe[3]. Its platoons ambushed the country around it: on 6 March a platoon at the road bridge on the Suoi Sau, near the Horseshoe, fired on a party of enemy, and two bodies were found in the morning. On 7 April a soldier of B Company set off a mine just outside a line the engineers had swept, and two Australians died.

There were a number of injuries and deaths during the mine-laying itself[3]. On 9 May an engineer of 1st Field Squadron set off an M16 mine while laying it, wounding six, two of whom died; on 20 May an anti-lift device killed two engineers; and on 30 May a member of a mine-arming party from 7 RAR's Assault Pioneers set off a mine that killed a sapper, recorded as friendly fire. In all, the record counts 7 killed on the Task Force's side and 10 wounded under Leeton, and 5 enemy killed. The minefield's security was not effective, and the Viet Cong breached the fences, lifted the mines and used them against Australian and South Vietnamese troops[3].

sources.title: Soldiers of 1 Troop, 1st Field Squadron, Royal Australian Engineers, working on the barrier minefield, May 1967 (P02115.001)
Dangers of patrolling during the Vietnam War
Book review: The Minefield – An Australian Tragedy in Vietnam
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

portsea.summary: 6 RAR, with armoured personnel carriers, catches the rearguard of a Viet Cong main-force battalion withdrawing across the Song Rai after its attack on Lo Gom.
portsea.text:
Portsea began on 21 March 1967, after an enemy attack on Lo Gom: the record says the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR) was set to intercept the enemy as they withdrew. On the first day half of a B Company platoon, checking a sandhill in dense scrub, was fired on from hidden pits at 5 metres; three Australians were hit and two of them died, and the enemy, six to eight men of 2 Battalion, 275 Regiment, slipped away under an airstrike and artillery fire. Next day A Company met a dug-in enemy platoon, the rear of that battalion covering its withdrawal across the Song Rai, and took the position behind heavy artillery and mortar fire as the enemy pulled out. The same dawn B Company and armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment caught five motorised sampans supplying the enemy offshore, sinking three; six enemy were recorded killed.

The rest of the operation was searching, most of it by patrols (9 of its 13 contacts). C Company found a booby-trapped cache of 80 tons of rice, and three of its men were wounded. Mines killed a soldier of 6 RAR crossing Route 23 south of Xuyen Moc, and one of 5 RAR north of Phuoc Loi, a US mine that the local sub-sector said it had not laid. On 5 April a scout fired at a figure who jumped out in front of him and killed a woman; the record classes it as a contact with civilians. In all it counts 4 killed on the Task Force's side and 9 wounded, and 8 enemy killed and 12 wounded.

lismore.summary: 7 RAR's first major operation: a week of patrols through enemy camps and bunker systems, with tracker dogs following up.
lismore.text:
The 7th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (7 RAR) began arriving in Vietnam in April 1967 to relieve 5 RAR[1]. On 2 May 20 helicopters dropped it into a landing zone to begin Lismore, its first major operation against the Viet Cong[2].

In six days the record holds 20 contacts, 18 of them 7 RAR's: mostly patrols (12), with security (6) and ambushes (2). They were small, sudden meetings with groups of three or four enemy on tracks and around camps and bunker systems, often followed up with tracker dogs, while artillery fired on the enemy's escape routes. On 3 May C Company heard firing close by and found four Vietnamese bound with wire and shot, three of them still alive, executed by the enemy. The record counts 8 enemy killed and 7 wounded, and one Australian wounded.

sources.title: Combat experiences during the Vietnam War

ballarat.summary: 7 RAR searches the Hat Dich area; A Company fights the Viet Cong 274th Regiment at Suoi Chau Pha, where six Australians are killed.
ballarat.text:
Ballarat, from 1 to 13 August 1967, was a search and destroy operation by the 7th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (7 RAR) in the Hat Dich area, where A Company was put in by stealth to ambush the trails to enemy camps.

On 6 August A Company's ambush killed two enemy, and its platoons following the track ran into a defensive position held by the Viet Cong 274th Regiment, the action known as the Battle of Suoi Chau Pha[1]. The fight lasted several hours, with seven enemy machine-guns firing at 30 metres, before the enemy withdrew north under air strikes and artillery; they had been covering their battalion's withdrawal from a camp a kilometre away. The record counts 6 killed on the Task Force's side and 19 wounded in that contact, and an estimated 15 enemy killed (five by body count). In the following week 7 RAR's platoons had smaller contacts with the local Chau Duc Company. Over the whole operation the record counts 6 killed on the Task Force's side and 19 wounded, and 19 enemy killed and 28 wounded.

sources.title: Combat experiences during the Vietnam War

ainslie.summary: Vietnamese families are moved to the new village of Suoi Nghe to deny the Viet Cong supplies, while 2 RAR and 7 RAR search the enemy's camps.
ainslie.text:
In Operation Ainslie, in September 1967, Vietnamese families were resettled in the new village of Ap Suoi Nghe, to deny the Viet Cong supplies[1]. Sappers of 1st Field Squadron pulled down and burnt the old houses, and the people moved south along Route 2[1]. The move was an attempt to follow the principles that had worked in the Malayan Emergency, though it came to be regarded as unsuccessful[2].

The record's contacts run from 31 August to 20 September, 28 of them: 11 were the 2nd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's (2 RAR) and 10 were 7 RAR's, mostly patrols (18) and security (7). The battalions found and destroyed enemy camps: on 13 September 9 Platoon of 2 RAR surprised a platoon of D445 Battalion's C4 Company in its camp, and on 14 September three enemy who slipped into a battalion-sized camp that 7 RAR was guarding while engineers blew it up were shot. A Special Air Service patrol's ambush killed three on the first day. The record counts 14 enemy killed and 9 wounded, and one Australian wounded.

sources.title: Book review: The Minefield – An Australian Tragedy in Vietnam
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

santa-fe.summary: Both battalions search enemy camps and bunker systems in the north-east of the province; 49 contacts, with night attacks on Australian positions.
santa-fe.text:
Santa Fe, from 28 October to 15 November 1967, took 7 RAR and 2 RAR into the north-east of Phuoc Tuy province, where the New Zealand guns of 161st Field Battery were among those supporting them[1]. The record also has the guns of 4th Field Regiment, armoured personnel carriers and the Special Air Service taking part. It has 49 contacts in the record, 29 of them 7 RAR's and 14 of them 2 RAR's: patrols (21), ambushes (14) and security (12).

The battalions found camps and bunker systems; on 7 November a platoon of 7 RAR came on a hut, killed three, and found nearby a camp of 12 bunkers holding documents, weapons and a radio. The enemy struck back at night: on 5 November they got through 108 Field Battery's defences and fired Claymore mines at its sleeping quarters, killing a gunner, and on 10 November a command-detonated mine fired into a 7 RAR platoon's base killed two Australians and wounded six. On 2 November those hit by a 7 RAR patrol's return fire at a creek were probably civilians: a boy and a girl were killed and an elderly couple wounded. The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 12 wounded, and 35 enemy killed and 11 wounded.

sources.title: Operation Santa Fe, north-east of Phuoc Tuy Province, November 1967 (COL/67/1120/VN)

forrest.summary: 2 RAR and 7 RAR hunt the local Viet Cong into January: a costly attack on a base camp, then ambushes of parties carrying food.
forrest.text:
Forrest ran from 25 November 1967 to 5 January 1968, and with 60 contacts it is the largest operation of these months in the record. 2 RAR (25) and 7 RAR (23) did most of the fighting, with the guns of 4th Field Regiment (13) in support.

It opened hard. On 27 November, acting on the Special Air Service's information, D Company of 7 RAR attacked an occupied base camp and took it, but the enemy circled back through their trenches and counter-attacked, firing rocket-propelled grenades into the trees above the Australians; two were killed and 22 wounded. The camp had been prepared by the Chau Duc District Company and was probably a forward base for D445 Battalion. The same day a booby trap in an enemy camp west of Xuyen Moc killed two of 2 RAR, and on 30 November a command-detonated mine and gunfire hit a 12-man 2 RAR patrol.

After that the operation was mostly ambushes, which caught small parties of Viet Cong carrying food and packs. On 2 December, by the record's date, 12 Platoon of 2 RAR killed four of six Viet Cong, among them the commander of the Xuyen Moc district platoon; the Australian War Memorial, which holds a submachine-gun captured there, dates the contact 21 December[1]. On 12 December a Special Air Service patrol killed all seven of a food-carrying party. In all the record counts 7 killed on the Task Force's side and 32 wounded, and 41 enemy killed.

sources.title: Chicom Type 43 Sub-machine Gun: Viet Cong (RELAWM40072)

duntroon.summary: Ten days in January 1968 in which 2 RAR and 7 RAR patrolled and ambushed, and 2 RAR's New Zealand V Company fought a four-hour night battle.
duntroon.text:
Operation Duntroon ran from 10 to 20 January 1968. The record has 21 contacts from it, almost all by the 2nd and 7th Battalions of the Royal Australian Regiment (2 RAR with 7, 7 RAR with 6), most of them on patrol (11), on security (5) or in ambush (3).

The heaviest fighting came on the night of 13 January, when V Company, the New Zealand company serving with 2 RAR, ambushed groups of about ten Viet Cong and began a four-hour battle in which two such groups clashed with it again and again, with artillery and a Spooky gunship in support. Sweeps over the next mornings found more dead and wounded enemy, and AK-47s, rocket-propelled grenade launchers, a machine-gun and packs were captured. On 14 January, as a platoon of V Company resited its Claymore mines on a track, two New Zealanders and an Australian engineer were wounded in the sweep that followed.

In all, 14 enemy were recorded killed and one wounded, and three of the Task Force's men were wounded; none was killed.

coburg.summary: The Task Force's first operation outside Phuoc Tuy: 2 RAR and 7 RAR, later 3 RAR, sent to the Bien Hoa–Long Khanh border to protect allied bases during Tet.
coburg.text:
Operation Coburg, from 24 January to 1 March 1968, was the first time the 1st Australian Task Force was deployed outside Phuoc Tuy province: the 2nd and 7th Battalions of the Royal Australian Regiment (2 RAR and 7 RAR) went to the Bien Hoa–Long Khanh border to protect allied bases during the Tet offensive[1]. Intelligence at the end of January suggested an assault on Saigon over the Tet festivities, and the battalions were placed along the Viet Cong's main approach to Saigon to block enemy troops moving back after their attack[2]. Their task was also to stop the enemy firing rockets at the military complexes at Bien Hoa and Long Binh[3].

The fighting began before the offensive did. On 27 January 10 Platoon of 7 RAR's D Company walked unknowingly onto a camp holding more than a company of the enemy, recorded as C238 Battalion concentrating to attack Long Binh; one Australian was killed and ten wounded before artillery, gunships, an airstrike and the rest of the company cleared it. On the night of 31 January the Viet Cong overran the village of Trang Bom, close to the Australian positions, and 2 RAR drove them out, then drove them out again after they came back[2]. The record has D Company, 2 RAR, carried in armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment with South Vietnamese troops, doing it: 11 enemy were recorded killed in the second attack, and six civilians were also killed by artillery. As the enemy withdrew from Saigon past the Australian positions, a series of ambushes in the first week of February killed 90 and captured five[2]. On 7 February C Company, 7 RAR, attacked a bunker system whose hidden bunkers opened fire at 10 metres, and 14 Australians were wounded.

On 11 February parts of the 3rd Battalion (3 RAR) relieved 7 RAR, and 2 RAR went back to Nui Dat on 13 February[2]. On the night of 18 February Fire Support Base Anderson, held by 3 RAR and an American battery, was attacked: the record describes at least a company of Viet Cong with a mortar platoon, which broke into the perimeter before carriers and the guns drove it back, and puts the Australian dead at seven or eight, among them four engineers killed by a single mortar bomb. Another account gives the attackers as a battalion of the Viet Cong's 274th Regiment[3]. In all the record has 142 contacts under Coburg, among them 3 RAR's fight to clear Ba Ria on 1 February, which it files here though it was fought at home in Phuoc Tuy. They count 20 killed on the Task Force's side and 123 wounded, and 230 enemy recorded killed and 74 wounded.

sources.title: Tet Offensive, Operation Coburg and the Battle of Ba Ria 1968
A Closer Look at US-Australian Operations in the Vietnam War: Operation Toan Thang I and the Defence of Fire Support Base Coral, April–June 1968
sources.publisher: Australian Army Research Centre (Australian Army Journal)

long-dien.summary: 3 RAR's B Company helps South Vietnamese troops clear Viet Cong from Long Dien during Tet; three Australians are killed rescuing a missing officer.
long-dien.text:
In the Tet offensive Viet Cong forces moved on Ba Ria and on Long Dien, about 5 km to the east; D Company of the 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (3 RAR), fought in Long Dien from 3 to 6 February 1968[1]. When the Viet Cong raided Ba Ria again, 3 RAR went back, and on the morning of 8 February moved to help South Vietnamese troops clear the Viet Cong from Long Dien[1]. B Company watched a South Vietnamese battalion withdraw under fire, and held its ground under sporadic contacts and sniper fire[1].

The record has four contacts in Long Dien that day, all by B Company. Its headquarters came under sniper fire from three trees, and a house into which one Viet Cong ran was destroyed with an anti-tank weapon; 5 Platoon cleared a house and captured an armed Viet Cong. Then 5 Platoon, sent to rescue a South Vietnamese officer and an American adviser cut off in the withdrawal, came under heavy fire from an enemy platoon; by the time 4 Platoon had joined it, the South Vietnamese officer had been killed, and so had three Australians[1]. The record counts three Australians killed and four wounded and nine Viet Cong killed, and notes that the enemy took a radio from an Australian signaller.

sources.title: Tet Offensive, Operation Coburg and the Battle of Ba Ria 1968

pinnaroo.summary: Six weeks searching the mined Long Hai hills in March and April 1968, mostly by 3 RAR with carriers and, for the first time in action, tanks.
pinnaroo.text:
Operation Pinnaroo took the Task Force into the Long Hai hills in the south of Phuoc Tuy from 1 March to 11 April 1968. The record has 80 contacts from it: 40 involving the 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (3 RAR), 13 the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment, nine the tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment, and six 2 RAR. Most (44) were on patrol, with 12 in ambush.

The hills were thick with mines. On its first day 2 RAR's New Zealand W Company set off two M16 mines in less than an hour; on 2 March, after B Company, 2 RAR, took the Dinh Co hill, an engineer set off a booby trap in the temple, killing himself and wounding 11 to 13 others. In the south-east of the hills on 22 March a chain of M16 mines killed three of 3 RAR's C Company and its engineers and wounded four, and two days later a platoon commander was mortally wounded by another.

The first Australian tanks, of C Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment, had reached Vietnam in February, and Pinnaroo was where they were first used in action[1]. On 20 March, when a platoon of 3 RAR's B Company was pinned down at the barbed wire of an enemy camp, a tank firing canister and machine-guns got it out, and the next day the tanks came back with B Company to find a large bunker system abandoned. Section ambushes by 3 RAR on 13 and 21 March each left four enemy dead. In all, 29 enemy were recorded killed and eight wounded, and the record counts seven Australians killed and 43 wounded.

sources.title: Australian Armoured units serving during the Vietnam War

toan-thang-1.summary: The Task Force goes north of Saigon to block the enemy's routes after Tet, and holds fire support bases Coral and Balmoral against North Vietnamese attacks.
toan-thang-1.text:
Operation Toan Thang I ("Total Victory") was begun by the Americans' II Field Force on 8 April 1968 to build on the defeat of the Tet offensive and set up a lasting belt of security around Saigon; the Task Force joined it on 21 April, first in the Hat Dich area on the Phuoc Tuy–Bien Hoa border[1]. When the enemy began a second offensive against Saigon on 4 May, the Task Force was given a more aggressive role: an area north of Tan Uyen, the "Catcher's Mitt", which the enemy used as a rest-and-supply area on the way from War Zone D to Saigon[1]. There the 1st and 3rd Battalions of the Royal Australian Regiment (1 RAR and 3 RAR) were to intercept and disrupt enemy forces withdrawing from Saigon and the Bien Hoa–Long Binh bases, patrolling from fire support bases that gave them artillery and mortar cover[2]. Unknown to the planners, the landing site lay on the forward base area of two North Vietnamese regiments, the 141st and 165th[1].

Fire Support Base Coral was set up on 12 May, about 7 km north of Tan Uyen, and was attacked in the early hours of the next morning, before its defences were finished[2]. The record has nine Australians killed and 28 wounded: a gun of 102 Field Battery and 1 RAR's mortar platoon were overrun and retaken, and 55 North Vietnamese were recorded killed. A second attack on 16 May, by an estimated regiment, was beaten off by 1 RAR, the guns and the carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment; the record counts seven Australians killed, the Anzac Portal five[3]. Tanks of C Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment, arrived on 23 May, and on 24 May 3 RAR moved about 4.5 km further north to set up Fire Support Base Balmoral[3]. Balmoral was attacked on 26 May by the North Vietnamese 165 Regiment, and on 28 May by two battalions, whose assault broke up on the wire; the record has 47 to 55 enemy killed that night. On their way to Balmoral on 25 May, tanks got their escorting infantry platoon out of a contact among enemy bunkers, the first time since 1945 that Australian tanks had fought in close support of infantry[3]. Outside the wire, tanks and 1 RAR fought into bunker systems again on 26 and 30 May.

The last Australians left Coral and Balmoral on 6 June; the fighting there since 12 May was the Australians' most costly and protracted battle of the war[3]. The record has 144 contacts for Toan Thang 1, half of them 1 RAR's (72) and 44 3 RAR's, with 29 killed on the Task Force's side and 118 wounded, and 265 enemy recorded killed and 81 wounded.
