horseshoe.summary: Contacts at and around the Horseshoe, near Dat Do, in late June and early July 1968, including a New Zealand patrol's fight at an enemy camp.
horseshoe.text:
The Horseshoe was a feature on the way to Dat Do, with checkpoints of its own, and the record files a handful of contacts under its name, from 22 June to 7 July 1968 and, three of them, at other times. Of those in these dates, the hardest was on 22 June, when nine men of a patrol of V Company, the New Zealand company of 4 RAR, killed three enemy and found they were at the edge of an enemy camp; attacked by at least 30 at close range, they held off further assaults with mortars, gunships and artillery until the rest of the company was flown in. One New Zealander was mortally wounded and three were wounded, and at least five enemy were killed and nine wounded.

On 7 July a section of 4 RAR's C Company went to help the northern checkpoint at Dat Do when it was attacked; a few Viet Cong mingled with civilians and opened fire, and the Australians could not fire back for fear of hitting the civilians. One Australian was killed.

merino.summary: 4 RAR, joined in the last week by 3 RAR, patrols and ambushes in July 1968, and ends fighting over defended enemy bunker systems.
merino.text:
Merino runs in the record from 1 to 24 July 1968. 3 RAR came into it on 18 July, redeploying from the Bien Hoa–Long Khanh border, where it had been in Operation Toan Thang II, into an area of operations named Yass, and it returned to Nui Dat when Merino ended on 24 July[1][2].

4 RAR's V and W Companies were New Zealand infantry companies; the battalion was formally named 4RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion[3]. Of the 29 contacts, 15 were 4 RAR's and 6 were 3 RAR's; most came on patrol (17), with ambushes and bunker fights (5 each), and the heaviest came at the end. On 22 and 23 July, 2 Platoon of 4 RAR's V Company, following tracks north through a defoliated area, ran into log-walled bunker systems held, it was estimated, by two enemy platoons, who fired rocket-propelled grenades and claymore mines down fire lanes cut through a fence. Artillery, helicopter gunships and air strikes were brought onto the bunkers; one New Zealander was wounded by a tree burst from the supporting artillery, and when B and W Companies attacked the next day the enemy had gone.

The record counts no Australians killed and 4 wounded, and 21 enemy killed and 9 wounded.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

platypus.summary: 1 RAR and 3 RAR search enemy country in early August 1968, and meet mines, claymores and defended bunker systems.
platypus.text:
Platypus is recorded from 29 July to 13 August 1968; 3 RAR's part in it ran from 2 to 13 August[1]. Its 36 contacts were shared evenly between 1 RAR and 3 RAR (16 each), on patrol and in security (11 each) and in ambush (7).

With air support restricted, 1 RAR's rifle companies relied on the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment for resupply along two trails, and the enemy noticed: on 2 August a carrier hit a large pressure mine laid in the previous two days, killing a trooper and an infantryman and wounding others, one of whom later died. On 4 and 5 August both battalions came up against bunker systems. A platoon sergeant of 3 RAR's D Company was killed as his platoon was pinned by six bunkers and a sniper. B Company, 1 RAR, went at a bunker system three times, with artillery and two air strikes between, and was twice hit by command-detonated mines; nine were wounded, one of whom died. Its commander admitted the company had not at first realised what it had met or how strong the enemy was.

The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 20 wounded, and 21 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

lyre-bird.summary: Engineers clear trails through the jungled hills west of Nui Dat, guarded by 4 RAR against small attacks and mines.
lyre-bird.text:
Lyre Bird was a land-clearing operation: engineers of the 1st Field Squadron and the 17th Construction Squadron cleared trails through 30 km of thickly jungled foothills of the Nui Dinh, Nui Thi and Nui Thi Vai hills, west of the Task Force base at Nui Dat[1].

The record runs it from 1 August to 1 September 1968, with 22 contacts, most of them 4 RAR's (8), guarding the work. The enemy's attacks on the work were small. On 1 August two men with a rocket-propelled grenade set a bulldozer alight and wounded its driver, and the engineers buried the burning machine to recover it the next day; on 2 August enemy creeping up on a W Company platoon guarding bulldozers wounded two New Zealanders. Mines did more damage: on 4 August a bulldozer of the 17th Construction Squadron set one off on a track off Highway 15, wounding two, and on 31 August an armoured personnel carrier hit another nearby, wounding four.

No Australians were recorded killed and 10 were wounded; 3 enemy were recorded killed.

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

nowra.summary: A Viet Cong company attacks the town of Long Dien and is driven out by 1 RAR; 3 RAR then takes over guarding Ba Ria and Long Dien.
nowra.text:
On 22 August 1968 an estimated 100 enemy, identified from captured documents as C1 Company of the D445 Local Force Battalion, attacked Long Dien with recoilless rifles, rocket-propelled grenades, automatic weapons and rifles. B, C and D Companies of 1 RAR were sent in with armoured personnel carriers, tanks and helicopter gunships, and fought until late afternoon, C Company and the armour inside the town and B Company on Route 23. Eleven or twelve Australians were wounded, seven of them by a single mortar round, and 29 to 40 enemy were recorded killed.

Operation Nowra followed: from 6 September, B and D Companies of 3 RAR relieved 1 RAR's companies in defensive tasks around Ba Ria and Long Dien[1]. The record's other contacts are small, the largest on 22 September, when a 3 RAR platoon coming down a hill met about 20 enemy coming up and had two men evacuated wounded.

The record counts no Australians killed and 16 wounded, and 47 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

hawkesbury.summary: 4 RAR and 1 RAR go to the Long Khanh–Bien Hoa border in September 1968 to disrupt the Viet Cong there and cut off their supplies.
hawkesbury.text:
Hawkesbury, from 12 to 24 September 1968, took the Task Force back to the Long Khanh–Bien Hoa border. 4 RAR deployed there on 15 September, and through patrols, ambushes and searches disrupted Viet Cong activity in the area and denied the enemy access to supplies, returning to Nui Dat on 24 September[1].

The record has 40 contacts, 4 RAR's (15) and 1 RAR's (14) almost equally, and many were ambushes on tracks (11). On 18 September a V Company ambush killed three men whose documents identified 3 Battalion, 84A Rocket Regiment, and on 19 September thirteen enemy, most of them unarmed porters, walked into two V Company ambushes; an identity card pointed to the D2014 infiltration group. The costliest fight came on 13 September, when a platoon of 4 RAR's C Company attacked what seemed an empty system of 20 interlocking bunkers and met very disciplined fire; three Australians were killed and six wounded. On 20 September 1 RAR's D Company found about 60 enemy in a system of 14 large and 10 small bunkers, and after an air strike and artillery cleared most of it.

The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 12 wounded, and 44 enemy killed.

windsor.summary: 1 RAR and 3 RAR are flown into the jungle of the Hat Dich for two weeks of patrols, ambushes and bunker fights.
windsor.text:
Windsor was a two-battalion operation that took 1 RAR and 3 RAR back into the jungle of the Hat Dich area, in the north of Phuoc Tuy, 10 miles from Nui Dat[1]. It began on 28 September 1968 with a heliborne landing by B Company, 3 RAR, into Fire Support Base Dampier on the Firestone Trail, with helicopter gunships firing to secure the landing zone in the middle of a known Viet Cong area[1]. 3 RAR's other companies followed over the next week, and the operation ended on 12 October[2].

The record has 31 contacts, 3 RAR's (16) and 1 RAR's (14): patrols (13), ambushes (8) and security (7). The ambushes took the most enemy. On 10 October a 3 RAR platoon harboured north of the Firestone Trail watched 80 or more enemy begin to file past and fired its claymores into them; two bodies and eleven drag marks were found the next morning. The bunkers took the most Australians. On 8 October a platoon of 1 RAR's C Company swept unsupported into a bunker complex held by an estimated enemy company and was pinned at 20 metres; two Australians were killed and five wounded, the enemy were too close for artillery, and a medical evacuation helicopter was hit before gunships could suppress the fire.

The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 10 wounded, and 24 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

capital.summary: 3 RAR moves from Windsor into Capital in October 1968, and 4 RAR and 1 RAR carry it on into November.
capital.text:
3 RAR went straight from Windsor into Capital, redeploying on 12 October 1968 into an area of operations named Garran; its companies came back on 21 and 22 October, in the battalion's last weeks before going home[1]. The record runs Capital on to 23 November, with 4 RAR (12 contacts) and 1 RAR (6) as well as 3 RAR (11).

Most of its 40 contacts were patrols (18) and security (10), and many were small and sharp: sentries and machine-gunners watching tracks into company positions, letting enemy groups come close and then firing. The worst came on 19 October. 2 Platoon of 3 RAR's A Company, in ambush 400 metres from its company base, killed one enemy soldier and ten minutes later was attacked by at least a platoon with rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns that tried to envelop it and then the whole company; two Australians were killed and six wounded before the company broke contact under helicopter gunship fire. On 31 October a 1 RAR reconnaissance party, seen as it approached an enemy camp, rushed it, and 18 bunkers were found in the area.

The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 9 wounded, and 31 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

capital-2.summary: 1 RAR and 4 RAR patrol and ambush through November 1968, ending with a costly attack on a large enemy camp.
capital-2.text:
Capital 2, from 10 to 24 November 1968, overlapped the last weeks of Capital. Its 35 contacts were 1 RAR's (15) and 4 RAR's (12), on patrol (16), in ambush and in security (8 each). North Vietnamese were about: on 10 November a 4 RAR platoon, after a fight on a track, saw about 15 North Vietnamese packs and heard the enemy organising an attack, and went into all-round defence under close artillery fire.

On 16 November a New Zealander of 4 RAR's V Company was killed when his platoon was ambushed from dense cover. The operation ended hard. On 24 November 2 Platoon of 1 RAR's A Company surprised about 15 enemy hastily preparing an ambush and followed them to a bunker complex of about 30 bunkers, around two years old; one of the platoon was killed in the first clash, and in the company attack that followed the commander of 1 Platoon and a section commander were killed.

The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 7 wounded, and 25 enemy killed.

goodwood.summary: The Task Force's biggest operation of the year: three battalions and armour in Bien Hoa and Long Khanh, against a feared Viet Cong offensive.
goodwood.text:
Goodwood was fought from 3 December 1968 to 19 February 1969 in Bien Hoa, Long Khanh and Phuoc Tuy provinces[1]. It was a reaction to a perceived threat: an increase in Viet Cong activity suggested that an offensive was being planned[2]. 9 RAR, newly arrived, joined it on 1 January[2]. 4 RAR joined it on 27 December and took part until 19 February, with a break at Nui Dat from 13 January to 7 February[3]. The SAS supported the infantry in mid-January[4].

The record has 257 contacts from Goodwood, the most of any operation in the period: 9 RAR had 89, 1 RAR 67 and 4 RAR 43, with the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (25) and the tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment (7). Patrols (103) and ambushes (65) were most of it, but the costliest fighting was against bunker systems (22 contacts), where the enemy waited with claymore mines and rocket-propelled grenades. On 10 January a platoon of 9 RAR's A Company fought a large bunker system for three and a half hours with artillery, gunships and air strikes; ten enemy and one Australian were killed. On 19 January a single rocket-propelled grenade landed among a section of 9 RAR gathered for orders, killing three and wounding five. On 16 February tanks and B Company, 4 RAR, attacked a bunker system; two Australians were killed and eight wounded, and one tank was hit by four or five grenades.

The record counts 21 killed on the Task Force's side and 108 wounded in Goodwood, and 181 enemy killed. The commanders drew hard lessons: not to manoeuvre near a suspected bunker system before the ground was examined, not to stand in groups, and not to be drawn into a bunker fight without heavy artillery, air and tank support.

federal.summary: After Goodwood, three battalions search and patrol Bien Hoa province through and after the 1969 Tet offensive.
federal.text:
Federal followed Goodwood in Bien Hoa province, from 17 February to 2 April 1969: searches and patrols after the 1969 Tet offensive[1]. 9 RAR took part throughout, with a rest at Nui Dat from 9 to 24 March[1]. 4 RAR joined on 19 February and left on 24 March[2]. 5 RAR, which had relieved 1 RAR in February, joined on 10 March and returned to Nui Dat on 8 April[3]. The record runs Federal to 9 April.

Of its 84 contacts, 9 RAR had 25, 5 RAR 24 and 4 RAR 13. The heaviest night was 23 February. W Company, 4 RAR, covering the approaches to Long Binh, beat off several attacks with claymores, closely coordinated artillery and an AC-47 gunship, and found six enemy dead and seven rocket-propelled grenade launchers at first light; the same night D Company, 9 RAR, answered rockets fired from about 600 metres away, and 15 enemy were eventually found dead near makeshift launchers. On 27 March two trucks of a US convoy escorted by carriers and 5 RAR hit mines on Route 15, and accounts of the wounded differ. On 4 April a platoon of 5 RAR's D Company, caught spread out in a bunker system with no reserve, lost two killed and seven wounded before it could disengage after four hours.

The record counts 2 killed on the Task Force's side and 46 wounded, and 78 enemy killed.

mat.summary: A 4 RAR Mobile Advisory Team ambushing with Regional Force soldiers near Dat Do is caught in the open paddy; an Australian corporal is killed.
mat.text:
By 1969, as the Americans began their phased withdrawal, the Australians in Phuoc Tuy were putting more of their effort into training the South Vietnamese Regional and Popular Forces[1]. The record files this one contact under MAT, a Mobile Advisory Team from 4 RAR. On 7 March 1969 three Australians of the team and 22 Vietnamese of 1 Platoon, 612 Regional Force Company, laid an ambush in paddy fields 150 metres from the tree line of Dat Do. Within 15 minutes the enemy opened fire from the trees with machine-guns, automatic weapons and B40 rockets, pinning the patrol behind the paddy banks.

Three Vietnamese and an Australian corporal were killed and two others wounded before mortar fire from 4 RAR at the Horseshoe stopped the enemy's advance; they withdrew, leaving one dead. The platoon had ambushed regularly from this spot and the enemy had come to know its movements, and the Australians thought the mortars would have driven the enemy off with fewer losses had the Vietnamese not withdrawn.

overlander.summary: 9 RAR and 4 RAR search Bien Hoa province in April 1969, with armoured personnel carriers, and fight through enemy bunker systems.
overlander.text:
Overlander was fought in Bien Hoa province in April 1969. 9 RAR, after Operation Overland on the Bien Hoa–Long Khanh–Phuoc Tuy border from 2 to 10 April, moved south within Bien Hoa on 11 April to begin Overlander, which for it ran to 15 April; these were reconnaissance-in-force operations, involving patrolling, land clearing and protecting civilians[1]. 4 RAR took part from 8 to 17 April, and then returned to Phuoc Tuy[2].

The record runs Overlander from 29 March to 17 April 1969, with 62 contacts: 9 RAR had 33, the 3rd Cavalry Regiment's carriers 9, 4 RAR 8 and 5 RAR 4. Bunkers were the hardest of it. On 8 April 12 Platoon of 9 RAR's D Company found a latrine and was fired on by an enemy platoon in a bunker system with a 200-metre front, cut fire lanes and snipers; seven were wounded, one of whom died, and by evening the company had cleared 25 bunkers with grenades. The same day A Company cleared 20 bunkers held by a platoon. The ambushes paid: on 5 April a section of carriers in ambush, with 161 Field Battery firing, killed six of about 20 enemy, and on 9 April 4 RAR's Anti-Tank Platoon killed seven.

The record counts 4 killed on the Task Force's side and 32 wounded, and 43 enemy killed.

surfside.summary: 5 RAR, with some of 9 RAR and armour, patrols and ambushes as the Task Force turns to pacification, and suffers most from mines and booby traps.
surfside.text:
Surfside, from 17 April to 2 May 1969, began in the month the Task Force made pacification its first priority: seeking out and destroying the enemy in its base areas, keeping him from the civilian population, and helping create a secure climate for South Vietnamese life[1]. Most of its 21 contacts were 5 RAR's (17). 9 RAR also took part: on 18 April its C Company was moving through dense jungle in Phuoc Tuy with a Centurion tank of B Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment, following in support[2].

The enemy's mines and booby traps did most of the harm. On 19 April an armoured personnel carrier working with 9 RAR hit an anti-tank mine made from an artillery shell, wounding four, and on 25 April two 5 RAR platoons set off a booby trap and a mine, wounding seven between them. The ambushes were small: on 30 April a 5 RAR platoon ambushing a raised footpath killed three enemy.

No Australians were recorded killed and 13 were wounded; 6 enemy were recorded killed.

sources.title: Dangers of patrolling during the Vietnam War

stafford.summary: 4 RAR's last operation of its tour: two weeks of small ambushes in late April 1969, without an Australian casualty.
stafford.text:
4 RAR came back to Phuoc Tuy from Overlander on 17 April 1969, and on 1 May it was replaced by 6 RAR[1]. Between the two came Stafford, from 18 to 30 April, the battalion's last operation in the record.

It was almost all ambushing: 14 of its 20 contacts were 4 RAR's, and ambushes (8) and patrols (7) made up most of them. Small groups of enemy walked into the battalion's ambushes night after night. On 28 April V Company's ambushes killed three of 8 to 10 enemy and captured a wounded man from the headquarters of 274 Viet Cong Regiment; on 25 April papers on a North Vietnamese soldier bore the unit number 2009. On 18 April a C Company platoon, supported by tanks, fired on enemy among houses and detained two civilians in a house where stores were found.

No Australians were recorded killed or wounded; 12 enemy were recorded killed.

lavarack.summary: 6 RAR's first operation: ambushing the enemy's routes across the north of the province, it defeats a North Vietnamese regiment's incursion in June 1969.
lavarack.text:
Lavarack was an ambushing and reconnaissance-in-force operation by the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, with its New Zealand companies, in Area of Operations Vincent in the west and north of Phuoc Tuy, from 30 May to 1 July 1969[1]. Its mission was to ambush the Viet Cong's major routes, among them the east-west route across the north of the province that linked the enemy's storehouses in Nui May Tao to its main force units[1]. The Task Force expected a quiet first operation for a new battalion, but on 2 June 33 North Vietnamese Regiment entered the province, a move the article judges primarily political: to show that the communists could enter villages at will despite the Task Force and the pacification effort[1].

In four battles from 5 to 12 June the battalion drove the regiment out of Phuoc Tuy, and it also ambushed 274 Viet Cong Regiment's supply and casualty-evacuation routes[1]. The record shows these fights. On 4 June A Company attacked a system of 19 bunkers, and on 11 June B Company attacked what it took for a small camp and found a large bunker system, and took ten casualties before it was ordered out. On 12 June V Company saw about 200 enemy carrying 20 to 25 stretcher cases and brought three teams of helicopter gunships onto them. On 20 June a D Company ambush in the Courtenay rubber killed 22 of about 60 porters and escorts. When 1 Battalion of 33 Regiment occupied Binh Ba, inside the area, on 6 June, the fight there was renamed Operation Hammer[1].

The record dates Lavarack from 2 May to 28 June and counts 83 contacts, with 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 24 wounded, and 104 enemy killed; the article gives 85 contacts, 102 enemy killed, and three of the battalion killed and 29 wounded[1].

sources.title: Operation Lavarack: Phuoc Tuy Province, Vietnam, 1969
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

twickenham.summary: 5 RAR ambushes and searches through May 1969, with one hard seven-hour fight for an enemy position in hillside caves.
twickenham.text:
Twickenham was 5 RAR's operation from 4 to 29 May 1969: 29 of its 30 contacts were the battalion's, and nearly half were ambushes (14). Part of the record files it as Twickenham/Toan Thang III. While it was under way the battalion spent 13 to 22 May outside Phuoc Tuy, sent to Bien Hoa province to meet an anticipated Viet Cong threat that did not develop[1].

On 5 May 1 Platoon of 5 RAR's A Company had three contacts on the same track: at dawn it ambushed a group that had stopped to eat before walking in, later it killed the first of about ten more who stopped to look at the remains of the last ambush, and a sweep killed an enemy soldier who tried to lure the platoon into a trap by moaning. Its company commander said the platoon had at last learnt to let the enemy into the killing ground before firing. The hardest fight came on 11 May, when the same platoon attacked uphill into a well-prepared position among caves held by about ten enemy and was pinned down in low scrub; 3 Platoon, sent to extricate it, came under extreme pressure too, and the platoon was brought out only after a seven-hour battle, with the help of a flamethrower. One Australian was killed.

The record counts 1 killed on the Task Force's side and 6 wounded, and 22 enemy killed.

reynella.summary: 9 RAR works in and around Dat Do in May and June 1969, where most of its losses come from mines and mortars.
reynella.text:
From April 1969 9 RAR's main work was pacification: seeking out and destroying the enemy in its base areas, and helping create a secure climate for South Vietnamese social, political and military life[1]. Reynella, from 8 May to 24 June 1969, was its operation in and around Dat Do; 39 of its 47 contacts were 9 RAR's, with tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment in 7. Part of the record files it under Toan Thang III.

Mines and mortars cost the battalion most. On 30 and 31 May clusters of M16 mines in Dat Do, missed by sweeps with detectors and bulldozers, wounded Australians of 9 RAR and a local civilian. On 6 June Fire Support Base Thrust, 9 RAR's headquarters, was mortared while its guns were firing for troops repelling an attack on Ap Lo Gom; one Australian was killed. On 24 June an armoured personnel carrier ran over a large anti-tank mine on a jungle track west of Long My and its two crew were killed; the record notes the tracks had been used too often. On 28 May enemy who had followed a patrol into a camp ambushed an engineer team checking it, and one engineer died of his wounds.

The record counts 8 killed on the Task Force's side and 37 wounded, and 6 enemy killed and 12 wounded.

hammer.summary: The Battle of Binh Ba: the Task Force's ready reaction force, with tanks and carriers, clears North Vietnamese troops from the village in two days of fighting.
hammer.text:
On the morning of 6 June 1969 a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a house in Binh Ba, a village less than 10 km from Nui Dat, hit a Centurion tank on Route 2[1]. The district chief asked for help, and the Task Force's ready reaction force, D Company, 5 RAR, went in with armoured personnel carriers of B Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, and tanks of B Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment, expecting to meet a couple of Viet Cong platoons; they met North Vietnamese troops[1]. The occupiers were 1 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, which had entered the village to show that the Task Force and the South Vietnamese government could not keep the communists out of the villages[2].

After a first armoured assault through the village the Australians came out, re-armed and went in again from the west, with B Company, 5 RAR, blocking; tanks blasted holes in the walls of houses and small teams of infantry went in, clearing them room by room[1]. The operation had begun as part of 6 RAR's Lavarack and was renamed Hammer that afternoon[2]. On 7 June an enemy company approaching Binh Ba from the south-west was driven off, B Company with tanks and carriers retook the hamlet of Duc Trung from a company of 1 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, that had overrun its defence platoon, and the Popular Force cleared the rest of the hamlet to avoid civilian casualties. A new sweep of Binh Ba that morning found the enemy gone from its western half, and the South Vietnamese Popular Force searched the rest[1].

The record counts one Australian killed and 10 wounded, and 86 enemy killed; the Anzac Portal says more than 100 Viet Cong and North Vietnamese, possibly many more, lost their lives, as did several South Vietnamese soldiers and a number of villagers[1]. Much of Binh Ba was destroyed, and Australian engineers and civil affairs workers began rebuilding it almost at once; the 1st Armoured Regiment, the 3rd Cavalry Regiment and the Royal Australian Regiment were awarded the battle honour Binh Ba[1].

sources.title: Australians in the Battle of Binh Ba 6 to 7 June 1969
Operation Lavarack: Phuoc Tuy Province, Vietnam, 1969
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

esso.summary: 5 RAR works around Dat Do and into the Long Hai hills with South Vietnamese troops, and loses heavily to jumping mines.
esso.text:
ESSO was a 5 RAR operation in the Long Hai mountains in which most of the Australian casualties came from 'jumping jack' mines[1]. The record runs it from 15 June to 13 July 1969, with 46 contacts, 38 of them 5 RAR's.

It opened with the worst of it. On 15 June, on the southern edge of Dat Do, a soldier of D Company stepped on an M16 mine that leapt two metres and burst among a platoon and company headquarters: three were killed and 20 to 24 wounded, and another mine laid in the previous two or three days was found nearby. On 4 July, on the south-east edge of the Long Hai hills, C Company found a bunker system holding mines; that night 7 Platoon hit an M16 mine, and a second went off while the wounded were being moved, killing three and wounding 14. Much of the rest was joint work with the South Vietnamese Army's 2/52 Battalion, handfuls of Australians patrolling and ambushing with its companies; on 24 and 26 June such forces were attacked by main-force Viet Cong and saved by helicopter gunships firing at close range.

The record counts 9 killed on the Task Force's side and 74 wounded, and 40 enemy killed; the Anzac Portal gives 9 killed and 58 wounded[1].

sources.title: Dangers of patrolling during the Vietnam War

matthew.summary: 9 RAR ambushes in July 1969; its commanders record hard lessons after enemy fire kills four Australians.
matthew.text:
Matthew, from 30 June to 18 July 1969, was a 9 RAR operation of ambushes (5 of its 11 contacts), patrols and security. Its record is mostly of lessons drawn after losses. On 30 June sentries of 6 Platoon saw three enemy approaching and went back to warn the platoon, as they had been briefed to; the enemy fired into the position and killed one Australian, and the commanders said the sentries should have fired. On 6 July 10 Platoon, withdrawing from an ambush position, was itself ambushed; one Australian was killed, and the company commander said the platoon had made too much noise.

On 12 July a section leader of 11 Platoon and his forward scout went 40 metres beyond their section into what was thought an old, deserted camp, saw bunkers, and were both killed when the section leader threw a grenade into one without waiting for his section. The camp, at least 75 by 175 metres and used for transit, was hit by helicopter gunships, mortars and artillery, but the enemy withdrew.

The record counts 4 killed on the Task Force's side and 3 wounded, and 2 enemy killed.

mundingburra.summary: The ANZAC Battalion works the populated south-east of the province, and the enemy's mines kill and wound more of its men than any fight does.
mundingburra.text:
Operation Mundingburra was the work of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, from 14 July to 12 August 1969. The battalion had come back to Vietnam in May for its second tour, had been joined by a New Zealand rifle company and renamed the 6RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion, and its main work was now pacification: seeking out the enemy in his base areas, keeping him from the civilian population, and helping to create a secure climate for the South Vietnamese[1]. The 101st Field Battery supported it, working with American heavy artillery[2]. The record shows two New Zealand companies, V and W, with the battalion.

The record has 41 contacts, 31 of them by 6 RAR: patrols (16), ambushes (8), security tasks (7) and attacks on bunker systems (4). There was fighting of the usual kind: on 19 July B Company attacked a bunker camp, losing five men wounded, and four enemy were killed; on 21 July V Company's New Zealanders ambushed six to ten enemy moving south and killed four. But mines did most of the harm. On 21 July an A Company platoon commander stepped out of a cleared harbour position south-east of Hoi My onto an M16 mine, which killed him and wounded 18; a second mine, set off while the area was being cleared, killed another soldier and wounded five, the battalion commander among them. On 23 July a mine killed two sappers prodding for mines in the northern Long Hai hills, and another struck a New Zealand platoon west of Lo Gom on a track the enemy had seen it use, and three men died. More New Zealanders were killed on 2 August by a booby trap laid by South Vietnamese Regional Forces, and on 12 August by a mine laid in an ambush position at Phuoc Loi after it had been swept that afternoon.

The record counts 10 Australian and New Zealand soldiers killed and 49 wounded, and 22 enemy killed and 11 wounded. The historian Greg Lockhart argues that from late 1967 to early 1971 the M16 mines lifted from the Task Force's own barrier minefield were the enemy's number one weapon in the province[3].

sources.title: Avoiding the issues: a reply to David Buring's review of The Minefield
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

camden.summary: 5 RAR works north of Nui Dat, fighting for the enemy's bunker systems in thick jungle and ambushing his tracks, with helicopter gunships, artillery and air strikes in support.
camden.text:
From late July to late August 1969 the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, worked north of Nui Dat on Operation Camden. The 105th Field Battery, flown by helicopter to Fire Support Base Polly, took part from there in 40 separate actions protecting an American reconnaissance-in-force and land-clearing operation north of Nui Dat[1]. The enemy's main force was back in the area: in July the headquarters of the Viet Cong 274 Regiment had returned to Phuoc Tuy, to a freshly renovated base camp north of the Nui Thi Vai hills[2].

The record has 50 contacts from 31 July to 29 August, 48 of them by 5 RAR: ambushes (18), patrols (15), attacks on bunker systems (10) and security tasks (6). Much of the fighting was for bunker systems in thick jungle. On 31 July a C Company platoon trying to take the flank of a system met 20 to 30 enemy and lost a man killed; on 8 August, after a briefing by a prisoner, the anti-tank platoon attacked a system held by an estimated enemy company and killed seven before breaking contact so that artillery, gunships and air strikes could take over; on 15 August a B Company platoon followed a telephone cable to another system, and five men were wounded by rocket-propelled grenades. The ambushes did well: on 6 August a D Company platoon, split in two groups, caught a column of 45 or more enemy on a track, and seven dead were found at first light. On 28 August an Australian shell fell short and wounded three of C Company's men; next morning the company took a camp of three new bunker systems, occupied by a regular enemy unit, without loss.

In all, one Australian was killed and 27 wounded, and 54 enemy were recorded killed and 37 wounded. The heaviest action of these weeks, on 21 August, is recorded separately, as Camden 2. The battalion's commander, Lieutenant Colonel Colin Khan, is recorded as lamenting that pacification was a waste of time and that the Task Force's proper role was to hunt the enemy's main force units in their remote jungle bases[3].

sources.title: Operation Lavarack: Phuoc Tuy Province, Vietnam, 1969
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

sources.title: Book Review - Fighting to the Finish: the Australian Army and the Vietnam War, 1968–1975
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

jack.summary: In the last months of its tour, 9 RAR ambushes around Thai Thien and runs into big enemy camps, mostly in October 1969.
jack.text:
Operation Jack (recorded in capitals, as JACK) was the 9th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's operation from 30 August to 29 October 1969, in the last months of its tour. The record has 41 contacts, nearly all in October and 40 of them by 9 RAR: mostly ambushes (17) and security tasks (13), with patrols (8) and a few contacts at bunker systems (3).

Some of the ambushes were laid close to the villages. On 22 and 24 October C Company ambushes near Thai Thien let groups of civilians returning to the village go by, then fired on the enemy who followed them or tried to slip past with the last group. On the night of 24 October A Company let the vanguard of a group of 50 to 60 enemy through, ambushed the group of 20 behind it, and brought artillery and a Spooky gunship aircraft down on the rest; reports of the result vary. The enemy's camps were more dangerous: on 2 October a platoon ambushing on the fringe of a large camp complex lost a man killed when the enemy counter-attacked, and on 26 October an A Company patrol was fired on at five metres from a bunker complex more than 200 metres deep, held by an estimated 60 enemy, who shot down a helicopter and hit a gunship and a medical evacuation helicopter. The forward scout was killed, and the enemy withdrew overnight.

Two Australians were killed and 8 wounded; 34 enemy were recorded killed and 29 wounded. Within weeks 9 RAR's tour was over: the 8th Battalion arrived in November and relieved it on 25 November[1].

burnham.summary: 6 RAR's September 1969 operation: patrols finding and attacking occupied bunker camps, and small, sharp contacts with enemy parties.
burnham.text:
Operation Burnham was the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's operation from 31 August to 30 September 1969. The record has 27 contacts, 19 of them by 6 RAR's companies, with the guns of the 1st Field Regiment, most often the 101st Field Battery, firing in support. Most were patrol contacts (15); eight were at bunker systems and four were ambushes.

The patrols found occupied camps. On 9 September the scout of a D Company platoon smelt smoke on a track just as the enemy opened fire from a bunker system, and a rocket-propelled grenade fired down the track wounded four men; after an air strike and artillery the company cleared the area and found 38 bunkers. The same day an A Company platoon attacking another system shot one enemy dead, drove off the rest and captured a wounded man trapped in a bunker. On 7 September a D Company platoon found an extensive, occupied system, withdrew, and left a section in ambush on its track, which killed two enemy. On 3 September an A Company platoon lost a man killed in a contact with an unknown number of enemy. Late in the month the contacts were with small parties: on 25 September the New Zealanders of V Company killed four of a group of 12 or more main-force enemy carrying cooking pots and rice, and a B Company platoon killed three Viet Cong.

One Australian was killed and 11 wounded; 23 enemy were recorded killed and 3 wounded.

kingston.summary: 5 RAR's companies find enemy camps and ambush tracks from mid-September to mid-October 1969, calling in air strikes, gunships and artillery on the withdrawing enemy.
kingston.text:
Operation Kingston was the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's operation from 15 September to 16 October 1969. All 23 of its contacts in the record were 5 RAR's: ambushes (7), patrols (7), contacts at bunker camps (6) and security tasks (3).

The companies were finding the enemy's camps and watching his tracks. On 20 September a D Company platoon smelt smoke at a creek and saw five Viet Cong in a camp on the far side; after a 15-minute firefight the enemy withdrew under artillery, helicopter gunship and air attack, and the platoon took the camp. On 30 September the same company's 12 Platoon drove enemy out of another bunker system, and an air strike, gunships and medium and field artillery were brought down on their escape routes. On 18 September the anti-tank (tracker) platoon, dropped off by armoured personnel carriers, met five enemy on a fresh track and found a Viet Cong staging camp nearby. The ambushes caught small parties: on 16 September a C Company platoon killed two of five enemy, one of them a woman carrying a radio, and on 16 October a section of the same platoon killed three.

No Australian was killed; 4 were wounded. 15 enemy were recorded killed and 9 wounded.

ross.summary: 6 RAR's search-and-clear along the Song Rai river: small contacts with local-force enemy, enemy camps found, and losses to a mine and to rockets.
ross.text:
Operation Ross, from 16 October to 26 November 1969, was a search-and-clear operation along the Song Rai river by the 6RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion; the 101st Field Battery was flown by Chinook helicopter to Fire Support Base Discovery to support it[1]. The record has 29 contacts, 18 of them by 6 RAR, and three by the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment: mostly patrols (11) and security tasks (7).

The companies found the enemy's camps. On 19 October V Company's New Zealanders bypassed a sentry and assaulted the camp of the medical group of D445 Battalion, capturing medical supplies and documents. On 8 and 9 November an A Company platoon, following footprints, came on a local Viet Cong base camp by a creek, 150 metres long with 19 huts and 19 bunkers, holding weapons, 1100 pounds of rice, ammunition, documents and clothing for 20 people. Most contacts were with a few local-force enemy at a time.

The losses came from rockets and a mine. On 22 October an armoured personnel carrier sweeping past a bunker complex with D Company was hit by two rocket-propelled grenades; one Australian was killed and three wounded, one of whom died three weeks later. On 25 October men of the mortar platoon and D Company, working with the South Vietnamese 3/52 Battalion, set off an M16 mine north of Lo Gom, and two Australians were killed and six wounded. In all 4 were killed and 9 wounded, and 5 enemy were recorded killed and 10 wounded.

kings-cross.summary: The busiest operation of these months: 5 RAR, with armoured personnel carriers and tanks, fights around the enemy's bunker systems for six weeks.
kings-cross.text:
Operation Kings Cross, from 31 October to 9 December 1969 in the record, was the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's biggest operation of these months: 85 contacts, 73 of them by 5 RAR, with the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (13) and the tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment (5) often alongside. The 105th Field Battery supported it from Fire Support Base Cape, north-west of Nui Dat, and fired a record 6,300 rounds in 16 days[1]. Patrols (35) and ambushes (21) made up most of the contacts, with security tasks (16) and bunker contacts (9).

The fighting was around the enemy's bunker systems. On 2 November C Company, riding on carriers, caught about ten enemy in a grassy swamp and killed six, and a B Company platoon, rather than attack a bunker system it had found, waited on a footpad leading into it and killed five of 12 enemy with machine-guns and rifle grenades; its commander concluded that ambushing a system's exits was better than attacking it. Attacks were costly: on 16 November a C Company platoon lost a section leader killed at the edge of a system of 20 bunkers and had to be extracted with artillery and gunships, and on 7 December a B Company platoon, outflanked at another system, held on until tanks and carriers arrived and destroyed the enemy who had not escaped; six enemy and one Australian were killed. The province's own troops fought alongside too: on 16 November South Vietnamese Regional Forces with B Company and tanks attacked six bunkers and killed four enemy.

The operation cost 4 killed on the Task Force's side and 20 wounded; 56 enemy were recorded killed and 41 wounded.

marsden.summary: 6 RAR searches rugged country for the enemy's base installations in December 1969, finding hospitals and tons of medical supplies, at the cost of five killed.
marsden.text:
Operation Marsden was the 6RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion's operation from 2 to 27 December 1969. The 101st Field Battery moved from Fire Support Base Discovery to Fire Support Base Picton for it, by road, leapfrogging its two sections of guns with armoured personnel carriers, tanks and air support[1]. The operation was a notable success: the battalion found extensive enemy hospital installations and seized many tons of medical supplies[1].

The record has 47 contacts, 37 of them by 6 RAR: patrols (21), ambushes (8), bunker contacts (7) and security tasks (7). The ground was hard: on 11 December steep slopes and gullies kept a D Company platoon's artillery from firing for 90 minutes after its section leader was shot dead approaching bunkers, and on 12 December another platoon found the sentry group of a large base complex, which was taken the next day after an air strike. On 18 December an A Company platoon following up a sentry post was hit by claymore mines, rockets and machine-gun fire, and its forward scout and platoon commander were killed. On 8 December an armoured personnel carrier travelling from Picton to Discovery, just north of Thua Tich, set off three anti-tank mines, killing a crewman and a sapper; the helicopter that came for the wounded landed on another mine. On 2 December two men of a D Company platoon were wounded by their own grenade-launcher round, which burst in heavy foliage.

The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 11 wounded, and 22 enemy killed and 9 wounded.

atherton.summary: The newly arrived 8 RAR learns the province through a month of ambushes and one hard bunker fight, over Christmas 1969.
atherton.text:
The 8th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, arrived in Vietnam on 17 November 1969, relieving 9 RAR, and joined 5 RAR and 6 RAR in the Task Force at Nui Dat; like them, it was to be mainly engaged in pacification[1]. Within a month it was on Operation Atherton, from 11 December 1969 to 10 January 1970. The record has 52 contacts, 47 of them by 8 RAR, and nearly half were ambushes (24), with patrols (15), security tasks (8) and bunker contacts (3).

The battalion's first weeks were not easy. On 12 December two enemy walked up to an A Company platoon still arming its claymore mines, and a rocket-propelled grenade wounded several men. On 21 December D Company found 30 to 40 well-trained enemy in six bunkers; one platoon, supported by another, assaulted them for 2 hours 40 minutes and beat off a counter-attack, and a soldier was killed trying to recover a wounded man. When the company came back with tanks next day, the enemy had gone. The ambushes did better as the weeks went on: on 18 December a D Company platoon killed three Viet Cong, two men and a woman, coming down a creek; on 31 December a B Company ambush killed two of three North Vietnamese; on 6 January a B Company section's claymores killed three of about ten enemy, and the platoon commander concluded they should be aimed low.

In all, one Australian was killed and 12 wounded; 28 enemy were recorded killed and 29 wounded.

bondi.summary: 5 RAR's last operation of its second tour: ambushes and standing patrols on the enemy's tracks, with no Australian killed.
bondi.text:
Operation Bondi was the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's last operation of its second tour, from 31 December 1969 to 14 February 1970 in the record. The 105th Field Battery supported it until 26 January, its own last operation in Vietnam[1]. The record has 40 contacts, 36 of them by 5 RAR, and most were ambushes (21) or security tasks such as standing patrols watching tracks (13).

The ambushes were small and quick. On 14 January an A Company platoon with only eight men in position, the rest away collecting a resupply, fired its claymores on three enemy and killed two. On 24 January a C Company ambush engaged eight enemy, and its sweep was fired on by the wounded; three Australians were wounded, and the platoon commander noted that the three M16 rifles in use had continual stoppages. On 6 February a dying enemy soldier's grenade, placed under his body, wounded four men of a D Company standing patrol when he was moved. On 11 February a C Company platoon stumbled on a bunker system held by about a platoon, fought for three hours until tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment attacked the bunkers, and that night another C Company platoon ambushed what were thought to be the same enemy, killing six.

No Australian was killed; 16 were wounded. 35 enemy were recorded killed and 19 wounded. The 7th Battalion arrived in February 1970 to relieve 5 RAR[2].

napier.summary: 6 RAR and its New Zealand companies patrol and ambush small enemy parties from January to February 1970, with no one killed.
napier.text:
Operation Napier was the 6RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion's operation from 11 January to 25 February 1970; the 101st Field Battery supported it from Fire Support Base Peggy[1]. The record has 60 contacts, 36 of them credited to 6 RAR and others to its New Zealand companies, which the record lists separately: patrols (28), ambushes (22) and security tasks (8).

The contacts were mostly with small groups of enemy on the move. On 11 January V Company, having found six packs, waited and caught five to eight Viet Cong coming back for them; on 13 January a V Company platoon's scout and machine-gun killed four of a group of 11 or 12, near a complex bunker system. On 28 January W Company's New Zealanders hit a party of enemy, and a prisoner said he and seven others had been trying to get into Ngai Giao village for food. That was what the ambushes around the villages were meant to stop: the Viet Cong's own history of D445 Battalion counts the Task Force's saturation ambushing around the villages among its most dangerous tactics, and says that because of the ambushes the battalion was almost never able to slip into the hamlets by night[2]. There were accidents too: on 27 January a grenade thrown in the dark bounced back and wounded four New Zealanders, and on 8 February a machine-gun jammed when the gunner's sweat rag was fed into it with the belt.

No one was killed; 12 were wounded. 41 enemy were recorded killed and 24 wounded.

sources.title: Book Review - The Viet Cong D445 Battalion: Their Story
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

hammersley.summary: 8 RAR, with tanks and carriers, fights for the enemy's bunkers in the Long Hai hills; a single mine on 28 February kills seven.
hammersley.text:
Operation Hammersley, which the Australian War Memorial dates from 10 February to 9 March 1970, was a reconnaissance operation by the 8th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, in the Long Hai area[1]. The record's contacts run from 10 February to 1 March: 38 of them, 30 involving 8 RAR, with the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (13) and the tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment (7) closely involved.

On 15 February a C Company platoon, set in ambush north of the Long Hais with 15 claymore mines, caught an enemy force of about a company, some 100 or more, and held on until tanks came out from Fire Support Base Isa; ten enemy were killed. On 18 February C Company captured a Viet Cong who said about 40 enemy were in a nearby bunker system ringed with anti-personnel mines. The company attacked with carriers and tanks; a carrier was destroyed by two rocket-propelled grenades and two Australians were killed, and a second assault, led by the tanks, was stopped by a deep creek and an anti-tank minefield and withdrew under fire, with 13 wounded in all. The same day B Company, rushed by carrier into blocking positions, lost eight men wounded by rocket-grenades, and a D Company platoon seven. Twelve enemy were killed in C Company's fight, mostly by the tanks, and the system was struck by B52 bombers before the battalion went back in two days later.

The mines went on killing. On 25 February a mine among a platoon headquarters of A Company, south-east of the Long Hai hills, killed one Australian and wounded two, and on 28 February another A Company platoon, moving through a known minefield with engineers clearing the way, had reached its ambush site when an M16 jumping mine went off among its headquarters, killing seven and wounding 13. In all the record counts 11 killed on the Task Force's side and 55 wounded, and 42 enemy killed and 34 wounded. The battalion received a South Vietnamese Meritorious Unit Commendation for Hammersley[1]. Its commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Keith O'Neill, came to conclude that operations in deep jungle produced bunker contacts that cost excessive Australian casualties for little permanent gain, and that operations around the villages were far more effective[2].

sources.title: Book Review - Fighting to the Finish: the Australian Army and the Vietnam War, 1968–1975
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

gisborne.summary: 6 RAR attacks the new base of D445 Battalion at the end of February 1970 and meets fierce fire from its bunkers.
gisborne.text:
Operation Gisborne, from 28 February to 9 March 1970, was the 6RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion's attack on the new base of D445 Battalion. The Task Force rated D445, nominally a local force battalion, as akin to a main force Viet Cong or North Vietnamese unit, and it remained a constant irritant to the Task Force throughout the war[1]. The record has 15 contacts, 10 of them by 6 RAR.

The first day was the hardest. On 28 February an A Company platoon moving to an ambush position was fired on by a three-man sentry group; another, searching for the camp, found a well-used track and a poncho before both its forward sections came under intense rocket-grenade and machine-gun fire, and nine men were wounded; the headquarters of D445 and its C1 and C4 Companies were in the area. A third platoon, trying to join them across the river, was driven back by fire from unseen bunkers. On 8 March D Company, under the command of 8 RAR, found nine bunkers guarding the northern approach to a larger system, and in two and a half hours of fighting three Australians were killed and six wounded before the enemy withdrew along prepared routes. On 5 March a Support Company section sweeping for a reported political meeting fired on a man and a woman who ran from it, killing the woman; the record lists this as a contact with civilians and notes the growing difficulty of telling Viet Cong from civilians working in the scrub.

In all 3 were killed on the Task Force's side and 18 wounded; 8 enemy were recorded killed and 14 wounded.

finschhafen.summary: 7 RAR, newly back for its second tour, patrolled and ambushed in Phuoc Tuy through March 1970, with 8 enemy recorded killed and two Australians wounded.
finschhafen.text:
The 7th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, returned to Vietnam in February 1970 for its second tour, again relieving 5 RAR, and its work was mainly pacification in Phuoc Tuy province: seeking out the enemy in his base areas, keeping him away from the villages and helping to create a secure climate for the South Vietnamese[1]. Operation Finschhafen, from 7 March to 1 April 1970, was among its first operations. Of its 24 contacts, 22 involved 7 RAR; units under the Task Force's headquarters and the 3rd Cavalry Regiment had one each. Most came while guarding night positions and harbours (9), in ambush (7) and on patrol (5).

The fighting was small and close. A platoon ambush beside a rubber plantation fired its claymore mines at stand-to at dawn and found two bodies at first light; a patrol shot two enemy running along a track; and a company headquarters, following signs of heavy movement into a dry creek bed, seriously wounded and captured an enemy soldier carrying maps. A combined Australian and South Vietnamese platoon from the Horseshoe met six Viet Cong and detained three young boys acting as their guides, whose questioning pointed to a possible camp for 27 Viet Cong. In all 8 enemy were recorded killed and one wounded, and two Australians were wounded, one of them a sentry who knelt up to look at what he took for a pig.

townsville.summary: 6 RAR/NZ and 7 RAR patrolled and ambushed in late March and April 1970, 6 RAR's last weeks before 2 RAR relieved it; 19 enemy recorded killed.
townsville.text:
Operation Townsville ran from 27 March to 19 April 1970. It came near the end of the tour of 6 RAR, which with its New Zealand companies served as 6 RAR/NZ; in May 2 RAR relieved it at Nui Dat[1]. The record holds 29 contacts, 12 by 6 RAR and 9 by 7 RAR, mostly in ambush (11) and on patrol (10), with a few at bunker systems (3).

On 30 March the Anti-Tank Platoon of 6 RAR/NZ ambushed the advance guard of an enemy party, and when the enemy fell back they ran into D Company and a troop of armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment placed across their escape route; five were recorded killed in all. On 8 April a platoon ambush engaged 10 to 20 main force enemy, killing three. Not every contact was with armed men: on 27 March a platoon met 13 people foraging for food, ten adults and three children, and three were killed and recorded as Viet Cong; the record lists it as a contact with civilians.

In all 19 enemy were recorded killed and 14 wounded. Two of the Task Force's soldiers were killed, a 7 RAR sentry who left cover to get a better shot at enemy coming along a creek line, and a New Zealand soldier in a contact at a bunker system, and three were wounded.

concrete.summary: 7 RAR's long operation of April to June 1970, with tanks and carriers: hard bunker fights and heavy ambushes, 52 enemy and 9 of the Task Force's side killed.
concrete.text:
Operation Concrete ran from 20 April to 17 June 1970 and was, with 63 contacts, one of the busiest of the period. It was above all 7 RAR's operation (49 contacts), supported by the tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment and the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (8 each), with 8 RAR (5) and the engineers of the 1st Field Squadron (2). Most contacts were ambushes (26) and patrols (17).

It began badly. On 20 April a carrier carrying 8 RAR troops on a track off Route 23 hit an anti-tank mine, killing a crewman and wounding ten. Two days later a 7 RAR company went into a system of 18 bunkers along the Song Rai to let a platoon evacuate its wounded, and met an hour of intense rifle and rocket-grenade fire; the troops were withdrawn, an air strike hit the bunkers, and by morning the enemy had gone. On 25 April a 7 RAR ambush saw more than 50 enemy coming and, supported by helicopter gunships, a Shadow gunship aircraft, tanks and artillery, recorded eight killed; on 30 April documents found after another ambush showed elements of D445 Battalion. On 21 May two platoons of 7 RAR went into an occupied bunker system on carriers, led by tanks, and fought through intense fire; one Australian was killed and 12 wounded, and five Viet Cong were killed and three captured.

Mines took a steady toll to the end: on 6 June a patrol following a blood trail in the sandhills south-west of Phuoc Hai set off an M16 mine laid where the enemy could expect an Australian follow-up, and three men died. In all 52 enemy were recorded killed and 24 wounded; 9 were killed on the Task Force's side and 61 wounded.

nudgee.summary: 8 RAR's ambushing operation of May 1970 in the paddy fields near Dat Do, with repeated clashes as the enemy fought to recover their dead; 31 enemy recorded killed.
nudgee.text:
Operation Nudgee, from 26 April to 10 June 1970, was 8 RAR's. It began four days after the Prime Minister, John Gorton, told Parliament on 22 April that 8 RAR would be withdrawn without replacement when its tour ended in November[1]. Almost every one of its 32 contacts was 8 RAR's (31), and most were ambushes (22), with the 3rd Cavalry Regiment's carriers coming to the platoons' help.

One platoon, 3 Platoon of A Company, fought again and again in the paddy fields. On 1 May, setting up an ambush, it was counter-attacked by 30 to 40 enemy, who withdrew towards Dat Do and the Long Hais; on 3 May it fought 40 to 50 Viet Cong for an hour, the enemy coming within ten metres to recover their dead and wounded, until carriers arrived, and six Australians were wounded; and on 14 May a party of about 15 Viet Cong walked into its ambush and seven were killed. On 29 May, after D445 Battalion attacked the Regional Force post at Ap Lo Voi, the retreating enemy, some 45 men, walked into the ambush of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, and fought back hard to get their men out.

In all 31 enemy were recorded killed and 42 wounded; one Australian was killed and 16 wounded.

capricorn.summary: 2 RAR/NZ's patrolling in late May and early June 1970, just after its arrival; mines and booby traps killed three of its men.
capricorn.text:
In May 1970 2 RAR began its second tour, relieving 6 RAR at Nui Dat; with two New Zealand companies, V and W, it took the title 2 RAR/NZ (ANZAC) on 15 May, and its main work was pacification[1]. Operation Capricorn, from 26 May to 12 June, came within weeks of its arrival. Of its 24 contacts, 12 were 2 RAR's and 4 were the Task Force headquarters units', mostly on patrol (9) and guarding positions (8), with four recorded as artillery and mortar fire.

The cost came mostly from mines and booby traps. On 29 May a platoon of C Company set off a claymore-type mine, possibly an M16, killing two Australians and wounding three, and the same day the forward scout of a W Company patrol set off two grenades tied to trees on a path round a rocky bluff, killing a New Zealand soldier. On 27 May an ambush killed two enemy carrying lights along a track, and on 2 June a W Company patrol, smelling smoke, swept through an enemy camp at the bottom of a steep, boulder-strewn re-entrant, killing one. In all 4 enemy were recorded killed; three of the battalion's men were killed and five wounded.

cung-chung.summary: The first phase of Cung Chung, from June 1970: intensive patrolling and ambushing across the province to keep the Viet Cong from the villages' food, taxes and recruits.
cung-chung.text:
Operation Cung Chung was part of the Task Force's pacification programme[1]. It ran in four phases from 12 June 1970 to February 1971, and set the battalions to intensive patrolling and ambushing to deter the enemy from moving through the area, denying him access to food supplies, taxes and recruits[1]. It limited the Viet Cong's ability to operate, but the constant patrolling put a strain on the troops[1]. The record files its phases under several names; this first, from 12 June to 11 August, holds 33 contacts, shared among 7 RAR (13), 2 RAR (8), 8 RAR (4), the Task Force headquarters units (5) and the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (4). Most were ambushes (10) and patrols (8).

The enemy's bunkers and mines made it costly. On 14 June an 8 RAR platoon was pinned by fire from two bunkers and held on for an hour before withdrawing for an artillery bombardment, losing one man killed; the same day an armoured personnel carrier carrying 7 RAR troops south-west of Long Phuoc Hai hit a large anti-tank mine, killing an engineer riding on it. On 18 June a New Zealand platoon of 2 RAR/NZ, investigating smoke, was hit by a command-detonated 105mm shell and by fire from bunkers down prepared fire lanes; two New Zealanders died and five were wounded. On 27 June an 8 RAR ambush killed four enemy. In all 12 enemy were recorded killed and 14 wounded; four of the Task Force's soldiers were killed and 20 wounded.

birdwood.summary: 7 RAR's ambushing around Dat Do and Long Phuoc Hai in early July 1970: 14 enemy recorded killed, 11 wounded on the Task Force's side, many by mines.
birdwood.text:
Operation Birdwood, from 30 June to 20 July 1970, was wholly 7 RAR's: all 23 of its contacts, most of them ambushes (15), in the country around Dat Do, Long Phuoc Hai and Hoi My. It ran within the first phase of Operation Cung Chung.

The ambushes were small, at night and at close range. On 1 July a half-platoon on the reverse slope of a sand dune west of Long Phuoc Hai killed two of five enemy crossing the crest, and the same night a patrol that saw five enemy by flashes of lightning sprang its ambush at 15 metres, though both its machine-guns stopped when mud splashed onto their belts. On 3 July a Viet Cong shot at a metre's range by the Reconnaissance Platoon's sentry was carrying a pack of explosive, which blew up and wounded two Australians. On 12 July a platoon that saw an enemy watching across the paddy towards Dat Do set an ambush at once and killed four local force enemy; one body had an M16 mine attached. Mines wounded others, three of them on 15 July south-east of Hoi My.

In all 14 enemy were recorded killed and 11 wounded; no Australians were killed and 11 were wounded.

nathan.summary: 2 RAR/NZ's operation of late July 1970 among caves and bunker systems, where mines, booby traps and bunkers cost 2 killed and 20 wounded, two commanding officers among them.
nathan.text:
Operation Nathan ran from 15 July to 10 August 1970. Of its 24 contacts, 11 were 2 RAR/NZ's, with tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment (2) and carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (1); most were on patrol (9), guarding positions (6), in ambush (3) or at bunker systems (3).

It was a hard operation for the ANZAC battalion. On 18 July a half-platoon patrol bumped a well-concealed bunker system and was hit by three claymore mines; documents from D65 were captured, and the company commander thought his men had had too little training in stealthy reconnaissance in small groups. On 26 July a New Zealand platoon of V Company, after following Viet Cong tracks for several days, was attacked with grenades, rifles and rockets among caves on rocky ground, and then hit by command-detonated mines as it checked the caves. On 2 August, as one platoon relieved another in a bunker system taken the day before, a booby-trapped 155mm shell went off while the commanding officer was showing his counterpart around; two men died, and both commanding officers were among the wounded and lost legs.

In all 9 enemy were recorded killed and 5 wounded; two of the Task Force's soldiers were killed and 20 wounded.

cung-chung-2.summary: The second phase of Cung Chung, August to September 1970: 8 RAR's night ambush outside Hoa Long killed 19 Viet Cong and captured six.
cung-chung-2.text:
The second phase of Operation Cung Chung ran from 3 August to 10 September 1970. Like the first, it was a campaign of intensive patrolling and ambushing meant to keep the enemy from moving through the area and from the villages' food, taxes and recruits[1]. Its 39 contacts were shared among 7 RAR (15), 2 RAR (14) and 8 RAR (4); most were ambushes (17) and patrols (13).

The outstanding result was 8 RAR's. On the night of 12 August a platoon ambushing Route 2 as a supply route into Hoa Long watched 50 to 60 Viet Cong move carefully into the village, let them pass, and moved its ambush to catch them coming out; they came back at about 3 am, carrying packs and much less alert, and claymore mines and four machine-guns caught the first group. Carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment pursued the rest. Nineteen Viet Cong were killed, six captured and one surrendered, with 550 pounds of rice, for one Australian wounded. On 14 August a combined ambush of 7 RAR and Regional Force soldiers killed four Viet Cong, two men and two women, at a track junction.

Mines and chance meetings brought the losses: on 8 August a mine in an enemy camp wounded seven Australians and a South Vietnamese soldier of 2 RAR/NZ's Anti-Tank Platoon, and on 27 August 7 RAR's Anti-Tank Platoon ran into eight enemy starting to build bunkers and lost one man killed. In all 42 enemy were recorded killed and 17 wounded; one Australian was killed and 15 were wounded.

cung-chung-3.summary: Cung Chung's long third phase, September 1970 to January 1971, as the Task Force fell to two battalions: 117 contacts, mostly ambushes, and 104 enemy recorded killed.
cung-chung-3.text:
The third phase of Operation Cung Chung ran in the record from 11 September 1970 to 31 January 1971, continuing the intensive patrolling and ambushing meant to deny the enemy the villages' food, taxes and recruits[1]. During it 8 RAR ceased operations in October and went home in November without replacement, leaving the Task Force with two battalions[1]. The phase's 117 contacts were 7 RAR's (50) and 2 RAR's (37) above all, with the 3rd Cavalry Regiment's carriers (16) and 8 RAR's last (1); ambushes (56) and patrols (36) made up most of them.

Several of the ambushes caught the enemy's food parties. On 15 December a 2 RAR/NZ platoon ambushing the house of a known Viet Cong food supplier in a rubber plantation killed 10 enemy; a prisoner later put the figure at 14. On 31 December about 45 Viet Cong walked into an ambush of 7 RAR with a section of cavalry; 21 were killed and nine wounded, among them the second-in-command and political officer of D445 Local Force Battalion, and documents of strategic value were captured, with no Australian casualties. In January 1971 two 7 RAR ambushes, one of them against a food party of the Long Dat district force, cost two Australians killed.

In all 104 enemy were recorded killed and 69 wounded; five of the Task Force's soldiers were killed and 30 wounded.

phoi-hop.summary: Ambushes and patrols by 2 RAR, then 3 RAR, from February to April 1971, the largest operation of the Task Force's last year.
phoi-hop.text:
Phoi Hop ran from 1 February to 28 April 1971. On 25 February HMAS Sydney landed 3 RAR at Vung Tau and took 7 RAR home[1]. Most of its contacts were by the 2nd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (2 RAR), with the New Zealand companies that served in it, and most were ambushes (44), with patrols (20), security (13) and attacks on bunkers (8). The record also files 14 contacts outside these dates under the name, among them 8 RAR's in 1970, before its tour ended.

Mines took a steady toll. On 1 February a machine-gunner of 7 RAR's Anti-Tank Platoon, in an ambush south of Xuyen Moc, rolled onto an M16 mine: five Australians were wounded, two of whom died. On 8 February a patrol of 2 RAR was hit by two mines, killing one Australian. On 2 March D Company of the newly arrived 3 RAR, still on its in-country training, was attacked in its harbour; a satchel charge killed its platoon commander and rifle fire killed another soldier. On 10 March a grass fire started by tracer set off a claymore mine during a sweep by V Company, 2 RAR, killing the New Zealand platoon commander.

The ambushes brought results of their own, often against small groups moving at night: four or five enemy who walked into a V Company ambush on 25 March lost three killed, and food, documents and medical supplies were taken. On 20 April 8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, attacked a bunker system held by 8 to 10 well dug-in enemy and had three men wounded before gunships and artillery took over. The record counts 6 killed on the Task Force's side and 18 wounded, and 51 enemy killed and 19 wounded.

briar-patch.summary: 3 RAR's first operation of its tour, from March to May 1971, against the Viet Cong's D445 Battalion and its mines.
briar-patch.text:
Briar Patch, recorded in two parts, was the operation of the 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (3 RAR), from 7 March to 23 May 1971, its first after arriving to relieve 7 RAR. The battalion had landed at Vung Tau on 25 February[1]. 3 RAR accounts for 49 of its 64 contacts, supported by armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment and tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment. Security (29) and patrols (13) make up most of the contacts.

The enemy the record names here is the Viet Cong's D445 Battalion. On 20 March a half-platoon of 8 Platoon, C Company, swept into a new bunker system; its platoon commander was mortally wounded and a helicopter gunship's co-pilot was killed by ground fire. On 31 March 1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, working under 3 RAR, ran into the headquarters of D445 Battalion and fought for two hours from three sides before withdrawing with nine wounded, two of whom died, one an RAAF crewman; 3 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon came to its aid and covered its withdrawal.

On the roads, mines were the danger: carriers of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, struck anti-tank mines on Route 328 near Thua Tich on 21 March, 26 March and 2 April. The record counts 4 killed on the Task Force's side and 15 wounded, and 6 enemy killed and 15 wounded.

overlord.summary: A Task Force sweep to the Long Khanh border in June 1971 to stop the enemy gaining a foothold in Phuoc Tuy, including the Battle of Long Khanh.
overlord.text:
In June 1971, as the Task Force prepared to hand Phuoc Tuy over to South Vietnamese forces, intelligence reports and Special Air Service patrols found North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces concentrating where Phuoc Tuy borders Long Khanh province, and they were believed to have set up a base near the Courtenay rubber plantation[1]. The Task Force commander, Brigadier Bruce McDonald, mounted Operation Overlord to stop them gaining a foothold in the province[1]. Signals intelligence placed the 3rd Battalion of the 33rd North Vietnamese Regiment and the Viet Cong's D445 Battalion there[1]. The 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (3 RAR), with the tanks of C Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment, was to search the area, while 4 RAR, a United States battalion and the armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, blocked the enemy's escape[1].

The record has 22 contacts between 5 and 13 June, most of them by the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (14) and 4 RAR (8). On 7 June, after a night of artillery and mortar fire on the bunker system it had found the day before, 5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, advanced and was pinned down 15 metres from bunkers held by part of the 3rd Battalion, 33rd Regiment. The fight went on for most of the day: the company's artillery forward observer was killed, a helicopter bringing ammunition was shot down and two of its RAAF crew died, and tanks of C Squadron attacked the bunkers from the rear before the system was secured in the late afternoon. This was the Battle of Long Khanh, and it seemed that the enemy had fought a holding action while their main body slipped away[1]. The complex had lecture rooms, dressing stations and sleeping bays for more than 120 people, and took engineers the best part of 4 days to destroy[1].

On 12 June three armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron carrying D and E Platoons were fired on by men of 274 Regiment; a rocket-propelled grenade set off claymore mines carried on the last carrier, which exploded, and eight Australians died. Later that day another section of carriers was ambushed nearby and two more men were wounded. The record counts 11 killed on the Task Force's side and 17 wounded, and 13 enemy killed. The Anzac Portal gives 8 soldiers killed and 22 wounded, 2 RAAF airmen killed, and the deaths of 6 enemy confirmed, and says the operation ended on 14 June with the enemy driven from their base areas in Phuoc Tuy[1].

sources.title: Australians in Operation Overlord and the Battle of Long Khanh in 1971

hermit-park.summary: 4 RAR, with cavalry and tanks, ambushing and clearing bunkers around the Courtenay rubber from mid-June to late July 1971.
hermit-park.text:
Hermit Park ran from 15 June to 26 July 1971, straight after Overlord. It was the operation of the 4th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (4 RAR), with its New Zealand company (23 of the 38 contacts), supported by armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, and tanks of C Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment. Half the contacts were ambushes (19), with patrols (12).

On the wet night of 21 June, carriers of 1 Troop, A Squadron, set ambushes along the southern edge of the Courtenay rubber plantation and caught an enemy force at 10 metres; 12 enemy were killed and three Viet Cong captured, with 22 packs and a large quantity of documents. On 25 June V Company, 4 RAR, found a large bunker system held by the 1st Battalion, 274 Regiment. 2 Platoon was driven back with three wounded, and 1 Platoon went in again with tanks and carriers against heavy fire from machine-guns, rocket-propelled grenades and claymores, with seven wounded; the area was not swept, so the enemy's losses are unclear. The day before, a New Zealand soldier of V Company had been mortally wounded on a reconnaissance.

In July the work was smaller ambushes and patrols, such as 7 Platoon, C Company's ambush of three enemy on 22 July. The record counts 1 killed on the Task Force's side and 13 wounded, and 35 enemy killed and 14 wounded.

ivanhoe.summary: 4 RAR's sweep against the North Vietnamese 33rd Regiment in September 1971, including the Battle of Nui Le, the last major battle Australians fought in Vietnam.
ivanhoe.text:
In September 1971, with parts of the Task Force already going home, the North Vietnamese 33rd Regiment was trying to establish itself in Phuoc Tuy; its units had been reported south-east of the Courtenay rubber plantation, and early on 19 September some attacked a South Vietnamese outpost and a nearby village[1]. The Task Force commander had to stop them, knowing that Australian lives would very likely be lost just before the Task Force withdrew[1]. Operation Ivanhoe, a search-and-destroy sweep south of the Courtenay rubber, was led by the 4th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment/New Zealand (4 RAR), with a company of 3 RAR, carriers of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, engineers and artillery; the tanks had left for home 5 days earlier[1]. The companies moved into the jungle between the enemy and the Long Khanh border, hoping to push them south onto blocking positions and cut them off from their sanctuaries[1].

The record has 7 contacts between 20 and 25 September. On 20 September a section of carriers escorting a vehicle on Route 2 was ambushed by about 20 enemy, and 11 Platoon, D Company, met about 20 North Vietnamese on a track. On 21 September came the Battle of Nui Le. D Company was fired on from a well-established bunker system of the 3rd Battalion, 33rd Regiment; its afternoon assault met intense fire 15 metres short of the bunkers, it withdrew leaving its dead, and it fought on until dark against a second bunker system, with artillery brought in close. Five Australians were killed and nine wounded, and 18 enemy were killed, nine of them by air attack. B Company, following a telephone wire, was mortared and had 15 wounded. Two days later D Company and V Company recovered the dead. On 25 September two carriers struck mines in the Cam My rubber.

The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 29 wounded, and 29 enemy killed. The Anzac Portal gives 6 Australians killed, among them a soldier killed on the first day when two Australian platoons mistook each other for the enemy, and 29 Australians and a New Zealander wounded[1]. They were the last Australians to die in combat in Vietnam[1]. The operation ended on 2 October, the last major Australian offensive operation of the war, and it succeeded in repelling the enemy's incursion into Phuoc Tuy[1].

sources.title: Operation Ivanhoe and the Battle of Nui Le 1971
